== History == [[File:Kinosaki1noyu01 2816.jpg|thumb|The monument of Ichinoyu and “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation”]]
According to the {{ill|Hot Spring Founding Legend|ja|開湯伝説}}, in 629 during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Shumei|ja|舒明天皇}}, the hot spring was discovered when a {{ill|Stork|ja|コウノトリ}} was seen healing its wounds. In the early {{ill|Nara Period|ja|奈良時代}}, in 717 (the first year of the {{ill|Yōrō Era|ja|養老}}), the Buddhist monk {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}} chanted the Hachimandara Sutra for a thousand days to aid those suffering from incurable illnesses; as a result, in 720 (the fourth year of Yōrō) the sacred hot spring burst forth, marking the legendary beginning of Kinosaki Onsen. One of the seven open-air baths, {{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}}, was so named. Moreover, {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}} is also recognized as the founding priest ({{ill|Founding Priest|ja|開山 (仏教)|lt=Founding Priest|lt_ja=開山}}) of Onsen Temple, which has since become a symbol of Kinosaki Onsen.
According to the Edo‑period {{ill|Onsen Ranking|ja|温泉番付|1=Onsen rankings}}, Kinosaki Onsen was ranked in the western division’s {{ill|Sekiwaki|ja|関脇}} (with the highest rank being {{ill|Ozeki|ja|大関}}—the western Ozeki being {{ill|Arima Onsen|ja|有馬温泉}}). In that era, nine tubs served as the origin for the open‑air baths. {{ill|Kōgen Jōnin|ja|弘元上人}}, known as the “Kūkai of {{ill|Tajima Province|ja|但馬国}}” (referring to {{ill|Kūkai|ja|空海|lt=Kūkai|lt_ja=弘法大師}}) and who served as the 50th and 52nd head of {{ill|Manpuku-ji|ja|満福寺 (養父市)|lt=Manpuku-ji|lt_ja=満福寺}} in Tajima (and associated with {{ill|Mount Kōya|ja|高野山}}), was originally from the venerable ryokan {{ill|Yamamoto-ya|ja|山本屋}} of Kinosaki Onsen. During the {{ill|Bakumatsu Period|ja|幕末}}, {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|ja|木戸孝允|lt=Kido Takayoshi|lt_ja=桂小五郎}} once fled to Kinosaki Onsen while pursued by the {{ill|Shinsengumi|ja|新選組}}. In the Edo period, Kinosaki Onsen featured not only entertainment venues but also numerous food establishments offering hot pot dishes, {{ill|Zenzai|ja|ぜんざい}}, {{ill|Udon|ja|うどん}}, and {{ill|Soba|ja|蕎麦|lt=Soba|lt_ja=そば}}, while fruits, fish, and poultry were transported from afar, and even delicacies such as {{ill|Pufferfish|ja|フグ}}, {{ill|Octopus|ja|タコ}}, and {{ill|Duck|ja|鴨}} were available. Rental shops provided items including the {{ill|Shamisen|ja|三味線}}, {{ill|Sugoroku|ja|すごろく}}, {{ill|Go (board game)|ja|碁}}, {{ill|Biwa|ja|琵琶}}, and {{ill|Koto|ja|琴}}, as well as weapons like {{ill|Spear|ja|槍}} and {{ill|Sword|ja|刀}}, delighting guests so thoroughly that they would forget to leave. Kinosaki Onsen was frequented by numerous feudal lords and retainers from neighboring domains, contributing to its lively atmosphere.
[[File:kinosaki_onsen.jpg|left|150px|thumb|Postcard from Meiji 43 (1910)]]
During the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|ja|日露戦争}}, a convalescent home for wounded soldiers was established, which also ended the severe economic downturn that had persisted since the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}. In the ensuing Meiji era, many prominent literary figures—including {{ill|Naoya Shiga|ja|志賀直哉}}, who wrote {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}, and {{ill|Takeo Arishima|ja|有島武郎}}—visited Kinosaki Onsen.
Around this time, the issue of private (inner) baths became prominent. In 1925 ({{ill|Taisho Era|ja|大正}} 14), the town was completely destroyed in the {{ill|Northern Tajima Earthquake|ja|北但馬地震}}; of the approximately 1,200 bathers present, survivors fled along the tracks and were evacuated by rescue trains toward the Keihanshin region. By the following month, as many as 82 guests were already visiting Kinosaki, and as long as the hot spring flowed, the crowds never dwindled. Much of the current Japanese‑style wooden, three‑story townscape originates from the post‐earthquake reconstruction or from buildings of that era; until the earthquake, ryokan did not have private baths, and guests patronized the open‑air baths throughout the town. In 1927 ({{ill|Showa Era|ja|昭和}} 2), when {{ill|Mikiya Ryokan|ja|三木屋}} (a lodging associated with {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}) utilized a newly discovered spring on its grounds to install the first private bath in a new building, legal disputes (the “Kinosaki Onsen Private Bath Lawsuit”) erupted over the perceived breach of local tradition, lasting more than 20 years. In 1950 (Showa 25), a settlement was reached allowing private baths with regulated size, while guests desiring larger communal baths continued to use the open‑air baths. Furthermore, all hot spring sources—including those on private property—were consolidated under the former Kinosaki Town “Yushima Zaisan‑ku,” and newly drilled sources began supplying private baths. In 1972, a centralized hot water distribution management facility—akin to a municipal water supply—was constructed to deliver water via pipes to each open‑air bath and ryokan.
[[File:Nishimuraya Hotel Shogetsutei Kinosaki Onsen Japan41s3.jpg|thumb|Private Bath (Reserved {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|露天風呂|1=Rotenburo|ko|노천탕|1=Rotenburo}})]]
These reforms led to the widespread installation of private baths in ryokan; today, nearly all accommodations offer them, though even in large establishments their scale remains modest. Because guests are exempt from paying for open‑air baths, “open‑air bath tours” while clad in yukata have become a signature experience.
In 1963, the {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ}} connecting the onsen town and the summit of Daishi Mountain was opened. In step with the period of high economic growth, a hot spring boom ensued, transforming Kinosaki Onsen into a major tourist destination. In July 2008, {{ill|Kiyamachi Lane|ja|木屋町小路}} was opened on a passage linking Kiyamachi Street and {{ill|Shisho Shrine (Toyooka City)|ja|四所神社 (豊岡市)|lt=Shisho Shrine|lt_ja=四所神社}}. In January 2015, a fire broke out that resulted in two deaths and the complete loss of eight buildings ({{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Fire|ja|城崎温泉火災}}).
Toyooka DMO ({{ill|Tourism Regional Development Corporation|ja|観光地域づくり法人}}), together with young ryokan managers and Toyooka City, established the Toyooka Tourism {{ill|Digital Transformation|ja|デジタルトランスフォーメーション}} Promotion Council in 2021. This initiative shares non‑personal accommodation and reservation data to analyze where tourists originate and to forecast demand months in advance, thereby informing PR and pricing strategies.
== Management == Kinosaki Onsen is managed by the Yushima {{ill|Zaisan-ku|ja|財産区}}, which not only owns four hot spring sources and six open‑air baths but also supplies hot spring water to 84 lodging facilities (for those outside the designated area, water is delivered by {{ill|Tank Truck|ja|タンクローリー}}).<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXLASHD26H0U_W5A220C1AA1P00/ |title=外湯めぐりで共存共栄 歴史の遺物「財産区」(3) |publisher=日本経済新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref>
== Open‑Air Baths == === Seven Bath Circuit === The open‑air baths comprise the seven baths: '''{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}}''', '''{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯}}''', '''{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}}''', '''{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}}''', '''{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯}}''', '''{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯}}''', and '''{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯}}'''.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/about/spa/7onsen/ |title=城崎温泉 7つの外湯 |publisher=城崎温泉観光協会|accessdate=2022-05-21}}</ref>
<gallery> File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan03s3.jpg|{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}} – Renowned as “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation.” File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan04s3.jpg|{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯}} – The bath of the elder sister of {{ill|Emperor Gotohorikawa|ja|後堀河天皇}}, known as {{ill|Yasuka Monin|ja|邦子内親王|lt=Yasuka Monin|lt_ja=安嘉門院}}. File:Kinosaki mandarayu2816.jpg|{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}} – The bath associated with {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}}, celebrated for a thousand days of sutra recitation. File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan09s3.jpg|{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}} – Japan’s largest station building hot spring, a modern facility also featuring saunas. File:Kinosaki yanagiyu2048.jpg|{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯}} – Water that gushes forth from beneath a willow tree. File:Kinosaki jizoyu2048.jpg|{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯}} – The hot spring of the locals. File:Kinosaki konoyu1920.jpg|{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯}} – Famed for healing stork wounds. </gallery>
=== Abolition of the Ichiban‑fuda === From 2002, the former Kinosaki Town Onsen Division and the Yushima Zaisan‑ku distributed an “Ichiban‑fuda” to the first man and woman to visit the open‑air baths each day.<ref name="kobe20210327">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/sougou/202103/0014188553.shtml |title=外湯巡りの「一番札」、人気で客が奪い合い 兵庫・城崎温泉やむなく廃止へ |publisher=神戸新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref> However, its overwhelming popularity led to disputes over order and even high‑priced listings on {{ill|Mercari|ja|メルカリ}}, prompting the Yushima Zaisan‑ku to decide on its abolition at the end of March 2021.<ref name="kobe20210327"/>
Yushima Zaisan‑ku and others are now considering the planning and sale of commemorative items that can be purchased regardless of order.

== Books and Onsen == Among the noted literary figures, {{ill|Naoya Shiga|ja|志賀直哉}} stayed for {{ill|Hot Spring Treatment|ja|湯治}} due to an injury and wrote the {{ill|Short Story|ja|短編小説}} {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}. In 2013, on the centennial of Shiga’s hot spring visit, the young proprietors of various ryokan at Kinosaki Onsen established a community‑rooted publishing label called “Books and Onsen”{{efn|August 20, 2013, certified as a {{ill|Specified Nonprofit Corporation|ja|特定非営利活動法人|lt=Specified Nonprofit Corporation|lt_ja=特定非営利活動法人}} ({{Corporate Number|5140005021403}}).}}<ref>[http://books-onsen.com/ Books and Onsen] (accessed June 2018)</ref>. The first issue comprised two works by Shiga (“In Kinosaki” and its annotations); the second issue in 2014 was {{ill|Manjome Manabu|ja|万城目学|lt=Manjome Manabu|lt_ja=万城目学}}’s 『Kinosaki Trial』, and the third in 2016 was {{ill|Kanae Minato|ja|湊かなえ|lt=Kanae Minato|lt_ja=湊かなえ}}’s 『Returning to Kinosaki』. All new works, these have been released exclusively at the local ryokan. They are printed on highly water‑resistant stone paper—made not from wood {{ill|Pulp|ja|パルプ|lt=Pulp|lt_ja=パルプ}} or {{ill|Kenaf|ja|ケナフ|lt=Kenaf|lt_ja=ケナフ}}, but from an {{ill|Inorganic|ja|無機物|lt=Inorganic|lt_ja=無機物}} {{ill|Mineral|ja|鉱物|lt=Mineral|lt_ja=鉱物}} powder—with towels available as water‑repellent book covers. Additionally, the {{ill|Kinosaki Town Literary Museum|ja|城崎町文芸館}}—opened in 1996—underwent a major renovation in 2016 for its 20th anniversary.

'''Kinosaki Onsen''' (城崎温泉) is a {{ill|Hot Spring|ja|温泉}} located in {{ill|Hyogo Prefecture|ja|兵庫県}}, {{ill|Toyooka City|ja|豊岡市}}, and {{ill|Kinosaki Town|ja|城崎町}}. Possessing a long history known since before the {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代}}, it was called “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation” (海内第一泉) during the {{ill|Edo Period|ja|江戸時代}}, a claim commemorated by an extant monument. Along with {{ill|Arima Onsen|ja|有馬温泉}} and {{ill|Yumura Onsen|ja|湯村温泉 (兵庫県)|lt=Yumura Onsen|lt_ja=湯村温泉}}, it stands as one of Hyogo Prefecture’s representative hot springs.
== Water Type == * {{ill|Salt Hot Spring|ja|塩化物泉|lt=Salt Hot Spring|lt_ja=食塩泉}}: {{ill|Hot Spring Source|ja|源泉|1=Spring Mouth}} {{ill|Temperature|ja|温度}} 37 – 83 {{ill|Celsius|ja|セルシウス度|lt=Celsius|lt_ja=℃}}. All the sources are collected in a centralized hot water distribution management facility built in 1972, where the average temperature is stabilized at 57°C, and then conveyed via a network of pipes to each {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|外湯|1=sotoyu}} and {{ill|Ryokan|ja|旅館}}.
== Onsen Town == [[File:161029 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan01s.jpg|left|thumb|Nighttime Onsen Town]]
Kinosaki Onsen is a hot spring town centered on a circuit of seven open-air baths. The foremost among these, {{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}}, was originally known in the Edo period as “Arayu” (新湯), but in mid-Edo, a practitioner of the {{ill|Kohō School|ja|古方派}} of {{ill|Kampo Physician|ja|漢方医}} {{ill|Shūtoku Kagawa|ja|香川修徳|lt=Shūtoku Kagawa|lt_ja=香川修庵}} extolled its water quality and renamed it “Ichinoyu” to imply it was the best in the nation. Also, {{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}}—officially known as the Toyooka City Kinosaki Onsen Exchange Center—is managed under the designated administrator system, with its bathing and training facilities run as a public–private venture while other facilities remain municipal; its premises also house the Toyooka City Kinosaki General Branch Onsen Division. At the seven open-air baths established in the onsen town, a token called the “Ichiban-fuda” is distributed to the first bathers of the day.
An onsen town is formed along the banks of the {{ill|Daitanigawa|ja|大谿川}} (Ootani-gawa), which connects the seven open-air baths from right in front of {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|ja|城崎温泉駅}}, and along the riverbank, {{ill|Willow|ja|柳|lt=Willow|lt_ja=柳}} are planted. Lodging facilities also line the main stream of the {{ill|Maruyama River|ja|円山川}} into which the Daitanigawa flows.<ref>[http://www.kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/shop/map.html 旅館・お店情報 » マップから探す] — Kinosaki Onsen Tourism Association (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> Moreover, the group of bridges spanning the Daitanigawa was designated as an {{ill|Important Structures for Landscape Formation|ja|景観形成重要建造物等 (兵庫県指定)|lt=Important Structures for Landscape Formation|lt_ja=景観形成重要建造物}} by Hyogo Prefecture in fiscal year Heisei 18 (2006). Located near the {{ill|Sea of Japan|ja|日本海}}, the hot spring is popular for {{ill|Sea Bathing|ja|海水浴}} in summer and for {{ill|Crab|ja|カニ}} cuisine in winter. At Kinosaki Onsen Station, there is also Satono-yu (a hot spring facility within the station building) along with foot baths ({{ill|Ashiyu|ja|足湯|1=Ashiyu}}) and hot spring drinking fountains ({{ill|Hot Spring Drinking Fountain|ja|飲泉|1=Hot Spring Drinking|de|Brunnenkur|lt=drinking hot spring}}), which are scattered throughout the town.
[[File:Kinosaki Onsen01s4592.jpg|thumb|Atago Bridge]]
At Kinosaki Onsen, wearing a {{ill|Yukata|ja|浴衣}} with {{ill|Geta|ja|下駄}} is considered proper attire. As of 2007, most ryokan here provide a separate yukata for strolling the town—distinct from those used as nightwear ({{ill|Nightwear|ja|寝間着}}) within the inn. Numerous shops in the town, identifiable by a signboard reading “Yukata Advisor,” (about 30 as of 2007) offer assistance when a guest’s yukata becomes disarranged, and some {{ill|Ashitaban|ja|下足番}} even lend their geta based on the design of the yukata.
A row of wooden, three‐story ryokan lines the street, and Toyooka City applies its {{ill|Landscape Ordinance|ja|景観条例}} to protect the area.<ref>[https://www.city.toyooka.lg.jp/shisei/keikaku/toshikeikaku/1003048/1003054.html 豊岡市城崎温泉地区における歴史的建築物の保存及び活用に関する条例] (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> In 2019, the commercial facility “{{ill|Nishimura Sanpō|ja|西村屋 (城崎温泉)|lt=Nishimura Sanpō|lt_ja=さんぽう西村屋本店}},” established via a city-wide solicitation project, was designed with wooden exterior walls to harmonize with the townscape. As of 2019, there were 74 ryokan/hotels—most of which are small-scale, family-run establishments with fewer than 20 rooms—focusing on individual travelers. In 2018, approximately 630,000 tourists visited, including around 50,000 foreigners; the proportion of visitors from Europe, America, and Australia (predominantly individual travelers) was about 30%, higher than in other hot spring areas (approximately 10%). To increase the number of stays of two or more nights, comprehensive improvements to the onsen town—including its commercial facilities and the {{ill|Kinosaki International Art Center|ja|城崎国際アートセンター}}—as well as cultural initiatives such as the “Books and Onsen” project (see below) have been implemented.
Additionally, a ropeway, {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ}}, operates nearby, offering easy access to landmarks such as {{ill|Onsen Temple|ja|温泉寺 (豊岡市)|lt=Onsen Temple|lt_ja=温泉寺}}, which is revered as the guardian temple of the Kinosaki Onsen area, and to the vicinity of the summit of Daishi Mountain where an observatory is located.

== History == [[File:Kinosaki1noyu01 2816.jpg|thumb|The monument of Ichinoyu and “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation”]]
According to the {{ill|Hot Spring Founding Legend|ja|開湯伝説}}, in 629 during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Shumei|ja|舒明天皇}}, the hot spring was discovered when a {{ill|Stork|ja|コウノトリ}} was seen healing its wounds. In the early {{ill|Nara Period|ja|奈良時代}}, in 717 (the first year of the {{ill|Yōrō Era|ja|養老}}), the Buddhist monk {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}} chanted the Hachimandara Sutra for a thousand days to aid those suffering from incurable illnesses; as a result, in 720 (the fourth year of Yōrō) the sacred hot spring burst forth, marking the legendary beginning of Kinosaki Onsen. One of the seven open-air baths, {{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}}, was so named. Moreover, {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}} is also recognized as the founding priest ({{ill|Founding Priest|ja|開山 (仏教)|lt=Founding Priest|lt_ja=開山}}) of Onsen Temple, which has since become a symbol of Kinosaki Onsen.
According to the Edo‑period {{ill|Onsen Ranking|ja|温泉番付|1=Onsen rankings}}, Kinosaki Onsen was ranked in the western division’s {{ill|Sekiwaki|ja|関脇}} (with the highest rank being {{ill|Ozeki|ja|大関}}—the western Ozeki being {{ill|Arima Onsen|ja|有馬温泉}}). In that era, nine tubs served as the origin for the open‑air baths. {{ill|Kōgen Jōnin|ja|弘元上人}}, known as the “Kūkai of {{ill|Tajima Province|ja|但馬国}}” (referring to {{ill|Kūkai|ja|空海|lt=Kūkai|lt_ja=弘法大師}}) and who served as the 50th and 52nd head of {{ill|Manpuku-ji|ja|満福寺 (養父市)|lt=Manpuku-ji|lt_ja=満福寺}} in Tajima (and associated with {{ill|Mount Kōya|ja|高野山}}), was originally from the venerable ryokan {{ill|Yamamoto-ya|ja|山本屋}} of Kinosaki Onsen. During the {{ill|Bakumatsu Period|ja|幕末}}, {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|ja|木戸孝允|lt=Kido Takayoshi|lt_ja=桂小五郎}} once fled to Kinosaki Onsen while pursued by the {{ill|Shinsengumi|ja|新選組}}. In the Edo period, Kinosaki Onsen featured not only entertainment venues but also numerous food establishments offering hot pot dishes, {{ill|Zenzai|ja|ぜんざい}}, {{ill|Udon|ja|うどん}}, and {{ill|Soba|ja|蕎麦|lt=Soba|lt_ja=そば}}, while fruits, fish, and poultry were transported from afar, and even delicacies such as {{ill|Pufferfish|ja|フグ}}, {{ill|Octopus|ja|タコ}}, and {{ill|Duck|ja|鴨}} were available. Rental shops provided items including the {{ill|Shamisen|ja|三味線}}, {{ill|Sugoroku|ja|すごろく}}, {{ill|Go (board game)|ja|碁}}, {{ill|Biwa|ja|琵琶}}, and {{ill|Koto|ja|琴}}, as well as weapons like {{ill|Spear|ja|槍}} and {{ill|Sword|ja|刀}}, delighting guests so thoroughly that they would forget to leave. Kinosaki Onsen was frequented by numerous feudal lords and retainers from neighboring domains, contributing to its lively atmosphere.
[[File:kinosaki_onsen.jpg|left|150px|thumb|Postcard from Meiji 43 (1910)]]
During the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|ja|日露戦争}}, a convalescent home for wounded soldiers was established, which also ended the severe economic downturn that had persisted since the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}. In the ensuing Meiji era, many prominent literary figures—including {{ill|Naoya Shiga|ja|志賀直哉}}, who wrote {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}, and {{ill|Takeo Arishima|ja|有島武郎}}—visited Kinosaki Onsen.
Around this time, the issue of private (inner) baths became prominent. In 1925 ({{ill|Taisho Era|ja|大正}} 14), the town was completely destroyed in the {{ill|Northern Tajima Earthquake|ja|北但馬地震}}; of the approximately 1,200 bathers present, survivors fled along the tracks and were evacuated by rescue trains toward the Keihanshin region. By the following month, as many as 82 guests were already visiting Kinosaki, and as long as the hot spring flowed, the crowds never dwindled. Much of the current Japanese‑style wooden, three‑story townscape originates from the post‐earthquake reconstruction or from buildings of that era; until the earthquake, ryokan did not have private baths, and guests patronized the open‑air baths throughout the town. In 1927 ({{ill|Showa Era|ja|昭和}} 2), when {{ill|Mikiya Ryokan|ja|三木屋}} (a lodging associated with {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}) utilized a newly discovered spring on its grounds to install the first private bath in a new building, legal disputes (the “Kinosaki Onsen Private Bath Lawsuit”) erupted over the perceived breach of local tradition, lasting more than 20 years. In 1950 (Showa 25), a settlement was reached allowing private baths with regulated size, while guests desiring larger communal baths continued to use the open‑air baths. Furthermore, all hot spring sources—including those on private property—were consolidated under the former Kinosaki Town “Yushima Zaisan‑ku,” and newly drilled sources began supplying private baths. In 1972, a centralized hot water distribution management facility—akin to a municipal water supply—was constructed to deliver water via pipes to each open‑air bath and ryokan.
[[File:Nishimuraya Hotel Shogetsutei Kinosaki Onsen Japan41s3.jpg|thumb|Private Bath (Reserved {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|露天風呂|1=Rotenburo|ko|노천탕|1=Rotenburo}})]]
These reforms led to the widespread installation of private baths in ryokan; today, nearly all accommodations offer them, though even in large establishments their scale remains modest. Because guests are exempt from paying for open‑air baths, “open‑air bath tours” while clad in yukata have become a signature experience.
In 1963, the {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ}} connecting the onsen town and the summit of Daishi Mountain was opened. In step with the period of high economic growth, a hot spring boom ensued, transforming Kinosaki Onsen into a major tourist destination. In July 2008, {{ill|Kiyamachi Lane|ja|木屋町小路}} was opened on a passage linking Kiyamachi Street and {{ill|Shisho Shrine (Toyooka City)|ja|四所神社 (豊岡市)|lt=Shisho Shrine|lt_ja=四所神社}}. In January 2015, a fire broke out that resulted in two deaths and the complete loss of eight buildings ({{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Fire|ja|城崎温泉火災}}).
Toyooka DMO ({{ill|Tourism Regional Development Corporation|ja|観光地域づくり法人}}), together with young ryokan managers and Toyooka City, established the Toyooka Tourism {{ill|Digital Transformation|ja|デジタルトランスフォーメーション}} Promotion Council in 2021. This initiative shares non‑personal accommodation and reservation data to analyze where tourists originate and to forecast demand months in advance, thereby informing PR and pricing strategies.
== Management == Kinosaki Onsen is managed by the Yushima {{ill|Zaisan-ku|ja|財産区}}, which not only owns four hot spring sources and six open‑air baths but also supplies hot spring water to 84 lodging facilities (for those outside the designated area, water is delivered by {{ill|Tank Truck|ja|タンクローリー}}).<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXLASHD26H0U_W5A220C1AA1P00/ |title=外湯めぐりで共存共栄 歴史の遺物「財産区」(3) |publisher=日本経済新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref>
== Open‑Air Baths == === Seven Bath Circuit === The open‑air baths comprise the seven baths: '''{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}}''', '''{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯}}''', '''{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}}''', '''{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}}''', '''{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯}}''', '''{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯}}''', and '''{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯}}'''.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/about/spa/7onsen/ |title=城崎温泉 7つの外湯 |publisher=城崎温泉観光協会|accessdate=2022-05-21}}</ref>
<gallery> File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan03s3.jpg|{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}} – Renowned as “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation.” File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan04s3.jpg|{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯}} – The bath of the elder sister of {{ill|Emperor Gotohorikawa|ja|後堀河天皇}}, known as {{ill|Yasuka Monin|ja|邦子内親王|lt=Yasuka Monin|lt_ja=安嘉門院}}. File:Kinosaki mandarayu2816.jpg|{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}} – The bath associated with {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}}, celebrated for a thousand days of sutra recitation. File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan09s3.jpg|{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}} – Japan’s largest station building hot spring, a modern facility also featuring saunas. File:Kinosaki yanagiyu2048.jpg|{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯}} – Water that gushes forth from beneath a willow tree. File:Kinosaki jizoyu2048.jpg|{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯}} – The hot spring of the locals. File:Kinosaki konoyu1920.jpg|{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯}} – Famed for healing stork wounds. </gallery>
=== Abolition of the Ichiban‑fuda === From 2002, the former Kinosaki Town Onsen Division and the Yushima Zaisan‑ku distributed an “Ichiban‑fuda” to the first man and woman to visit the open‑air baths each day.<ref name="kobe20210327">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/sougou/202103/0014188553.shtml |title=外湯巡りの「一番札」、人気で客が奪い合い 兵庫・城崎温泉やむなく廃止へ |publisher=神戸新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref> However, its overwhelming popularity led to disputes over order and even high‑priced listings on {{ill|Mercari|ja|メルカリ}}, prompting the Yushima Zaisan‑ku to decide on its abolition at the end of March 2021.<ref name="kobe20210327"/>
Yushima Zaisan‑ku and others are now considering the planning and sale of commemorative items that can be purchased regardless of order.

== Books and Onsen == Among the noted literary figures, {{ill|Naoya Shiga|ja|志賀直哉}} stayed for {{ill|Hot Spring Treatment|ja|湯治}} due to an injury and wrote the {{ill|Short Story|ja|短編小説}} {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}. In 2013, on the centennial of Shiga’s hot spring visit, the young proprietors of various ryokan at Kinosaki Onsen established a community‑rooted publishing label called “Books and Onsen”{{efn|August 20, 2013, certified as a {{ill|Specified Nonprofit Corporation|ja|特定非営利活動法人|lt=Specified Nonprofit Corporation|lt_ja=特定非営利活動法人}} ({{Corporate Number|5140005021403}}).}}<ref>[http://books-onsen.com/ Books and Onsen] (accessed June 2018)</ref>. The first issue comprised two works by Shiga (“In Kinosaki” and its annotations); the second issue in 2014 was {{ill|Manjome Manabu|ja|万城目学|lt=Manjome Manabu|lt_ja=万城目学}}’s 『Kinosaki Trial』, and the third in 2016 was {{ill|Kanae Minato|ja|湊かなえ|lt=Kanae Minato|lt_ja=湊かなえ}}’s 『Returning to Kinosaki』. All new works, these have been released exclusively at the local ryokan. They are printed on highly water‑resistant stone paper—made not from wood {{ill|Pulp|ja|パルプ|lt=Pulp|lt_ja=パルプ}} or {{ill|Kenaf|ja|ケナフ|lt=Kenaf|lt_ja=ケナフ}}, but from an {{ill|Inorganic|ja|無機物|lt=Inorganic|lt_ja=無機物}} {{ill|Mineral|ja|鉱物|lt=Mineral|lt_ja=鉱物}} powder—with towels available as water‑repellent book covers. Additionally, the {{ill|Kinosaki Town Literary Museum|ja|城崎町文芸館}}—opened in 1996—underwent a major renovation in 2016 for its 20th anniversary.

'''Kinosaki Onsen''' (城崎温泉) is a {{ill|Hot Spring|ja|温泉}} located in {{ill|Hyogo Prefecture|ja|兵庫県}}, {{ill|Toyooka City|ja|豊岡市}}, and {{ill|Kinosaki Town|ja|城崎町}}. Possessing a long history known since before the {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代}}, it was called “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation” (海内第一泉) during the {{ill|Edo Period|ja|江戸時代}}, a claim commemorated by an extant monument. Along with {{ill|Arima Onsen|ja|有馬温泉}} and {{ill|Yumura Onsen|ja|湯村温泉 (兵庫県)|lt=Yumura Onsen|lt_ja=湯村温泉}}, it stands as one of Hyogo Prefecture’s representative hot springs.
== Water Type == * {{ill|Salt Hot Spring|ja|塩化物泉|lt=Salt Hot Spring|lt_ja=食塩泉}}: {{ill|Hot Spring Source|ja|源泉|1=Spring Mouth}} {{ill|Temperature|ja|温度}} 37 – 83 {{ill|Celsius|ja|セルシウス度|lt=Celsius|lt_ja=℃}}. All the sources are collected in a centralized hot water distribution management facility built in 1972, where the average temperature is stabilized at 57°C, and then conveyed via a network of pipes to each {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|外湯|1=sotoyu}} and {{ill|Ryokan|ja|旅館}}.
== Onsen Town == [[File:161029 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan01s.jpg|left|thumb|Nighttime Onsen Town]]
Kinosaki Onsen is a hot spring town centered on a circuit of seven open-air baths. The foremost among these, {{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}}, was originally known in the Edo period as “Arayu” (新湯), but in mid-Edo, a practitioner of the {{ill|Kohō School|ja|古方派}} of {{ill|Kampo Physician|ja|漢方医}} {{ill|Shūtoku Kagawa|ja|香川修徳|lt=Shūtoku Kagawa|lt_ja=香川修庵}} extolled its water quality and renamed it “Ichinoyu” to imply it was the best in the nation. Also, {{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}}—officially known as the Toyooka City Kinosaki Onsen Exchange Center—is managed under the designated administrator system, with its bathing and training facilities run as a public–private venture while other facilities remain municipal; its premises also house the Toyooka City Kinosaki General Branch Onsen Division. At the seven open-air baths established in the onsen town, a token called the “Ichiban-fuda” is distributed to the first bathers of the day.
An onsen town is formed along the banks of the {{ill|Daitanigawa|ja|大谿川}} (Ootani-gawa), which connects the seven open-air baths from right in front of {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|ja|城崎温泉駅}}, and along the riverbank, {{ill|Willow|ja|柳|lt=Willow|lt_ja=柳}} are planted. Lodging facilities also line the main stream of the {{ill|Maruyama River|ja|円山川}} into which the Daitanigawa flows.<ref>[http://www.kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/shop/map.html 旅館・お店情報 » マップから探す] — Kinosaki Onsen Tourism Association (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> Moreover, the group of bridges spanning the Daitanigawa was designated as an {{ill|Important Structures for Landscape Formation|ja|景観形成重要建造物等 (兵庫県指定)|lt=Important Structures for Landscape Formation|lt_ja=景観形成重要建造物}} by Hyogo Prefecture in fiscal year Heisei 18 (2006). Located near the {{ill|Sea of Japan|ja|日本海}}, the hot spring is popular for {{ill|Sea Bathing|ja|海水浴}} in summer and for {{ill|Crab|ja|カニ}} cuisine in winter. At Kinosaki Onsen Station, there is also Satono-yu (a hot spring facility within the station building) along with foot baths ({{ill|Ashiyu|ja|足湯|1=Ashiyu}}) and hot spring drinking fountains ({{ill|Hot Spring Drinking Fountain|ja|飲泉|1=Hot Spring Drinking|de|Brunnenkur|lt=drinking hot spring}}), which are scattered throughout the town.
[[File:Kinosaki Onsen01s4592.jpg|thumb|Atago Bridge]]
At Kinosaki Onsen, wearing a {{ill|Yukata|ja|浴衣}} with {{ill|Geta|ja|下駄}} is considered proper attire. As of 2007, most ryokan here provide a separate yukata for strolling the town—distinct from those used as nightwear ({{ill|Nightwear|ja|寝間着}}) within the inn. Numerous shops in the town, identifiable by a signboard reading “Yukata Advisor,” (about 30 as of 2007) offer assistance when a guest’s yukata becomes disarranged, and some {{ill|Ashitaban|ja|下足番}} even lend their geta based on the design of the yukata.
A row of wooden, three‐story ryokan lines the street, and Toyooka City applies its {{ill|Landscape Ordinance|ja|景観条例}} to protect the area.<ref>[https://www.city.toyooka.lg.jp/shisei/keikaku/toshikeikaku/1003048/1003054.html 豊岡市城崎温泉地区における歴史的建築物の保存及び活用に関する条例] (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> In 2019, the commercial facility “{{ill|Nishimura Sanpō|ja|西村屋 (城崎温泉)|lt=Nishimura Sanpō|lt_ja=さんぽう西村屋本店}},” established via a city-wide solicitation project, was designed with wooden exterior walls to harmonize with the townscape. As of 2019, there were 74 ryokan/hotels—most of which are small-scale, family-run establishments with fewer than 20 rooms—focusing on individual travelers. In 2018, approximately 630,000 tourists visited, including around 50,000 foreigners; the proportion of visitors from Europe, America, and Australia (predominantly individual travelers) was about 30%, higher than in other hot spring areas (approximately 10%). To increase the number of stays of two or more nights, comprehensive improvements to the onsen town—including its commercial facilities and the {{ill|Kinosaki International Art Center|ja|城崎国際アートセンター}}—as well as cultural initiatives such as the “Books and Onsen” project (see below) have been implemented.
Additionally, a ropeway, {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ}}, operates nearby, offering easy access to landmarks such as {{ill|Onsen Temple|ja|温泉寺 (豊岡市)|lt=Onsen Temple|lt_ja=温泉寺}}, which is revered as the guardian temple of the Kinosaki Onsen area, and to the vicinity of the summit of Daishi Mountain where an observatory is located.
<gallery widths="160px" heights="110px"> Kinosaki onsen04 1920.jpg|Overview of the Onsen Town 一番札.jpg|Ichiban‑fuda 100722 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan03s3.jpg|Station Street Kinosaki onsen01 2816.jpg|Yunosato Street (the front right is “{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯}}”) </gallery>
== History == [[File:Kinosaki1noyu01 2816.jpg|thumb|The monument of Ichinoyu and “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation”]]
According to the {{ill|Hot Spring Founding Legend|ja|開湯伝説}}, in 629 during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Shumei|ja|舒明天皇}}, the hot spring was discovered when a {{ill|Stork|ja|コウノトリ}} was seen healing its wounds. In the early {{ill|Nara Period|ja|奈良時代}}, in 717 (the first year of the {{ill|Yōrō Era|ja|養老}}), the Buddhist monk {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}} chanted the Hachimandara Sutra for a thousand days to aid those suffering from incurable illnesses; as a result, in 720 (the fourth year of Yōrō) the sacred hot spring burst forth, marking the legendary beginning of Kinosaki Onsen. One of the seven open-air baths, {{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}}, was so named. Moreover, {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}} is also recognized as the founding priest ({{ill|Founding Priest|ja|開山 (仏教)|lt=Founding Priest|lt_ja=開山}}) of Onsen Temple, which has since become a symbol of Kinosaki Onsen.
According to the Edo‑period {{ill|Onsen Ranking|ja|温泉番付|1=Onsen rankings}}, Kinosaki Onsen was ranked in the western division’s {{ill|Sekiwaki|ja|関脇}} (with the highest rank being {{ill|Ozeki|ja|大関}}—the western Ozeki being {{ill|Arima Onsen|ja|有馬温泉}}). In that era, nine tubs served as the origin for the open‑air baths. {{ill|Kōgen Jōnin|ja|弘元上人}}, known as the “Kūkai of {{ill|Tajima Province|ja|但馬国}}” (referring to {{ill|Kūkai|ja|空海|lt=Kūkai|lt_ja=弘法大師}}) and who served as the 50th and 52nd head of {{ill|Manpuku-ji|ja|満福寺 (養父市)|lt=Manpuku-ji|lt_ja=満福寺}} in Tajima (and associated with {{ill|Mount Kōya|ja|高野山}}), was originally from the venerable ryokan {{ill|Yamamoto-ya|ja|山本屋}} of Kinosaki Onsen. During the {{ill|Bakumatsu Period|ja|幕末}}, {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|ja|木戸孝允|lt=Kido Takayoshi|lt_ja=桂小五郎}} once fled to Kinosaki Onsen while pursued by the {{ill|Shinsengumi|ja|新選組}}. In the Edo period, Kinosaki Onsen featured not only entertainment venues but also numerous food establishments offering hot pot dishes, {{ill|Zenzai|ja|ぜんざい}}, {{ill|Udon|ja|うどん}}, and {{ill|Soba|ja|蕎麦|lt=Soba|lt_ja=そば}}, while fruits, fish, and poultry were transported from afar, and even delicacies such as {{ill|Pufferfish|ja|フグ}}, {{ill|Octopus|ja|タコ}}, and {{ill|Duck|ja|鴨}} were available. Rental shops provided items including the {{ill|Shamisen|ja|三味線}}, {{ill|Sugoroku|ja|すごろく}}, {{ill|Go (board game)|ja|碁}}, {{ill|Biwa|ja|琵琶}}, and {{ill|Koto|ja|琴}}, as well as weapons like {{ill|Spear|ja|槍}} and {{ill|Sword|ja|刀}}, delighting guests so thoroughly that they would forget to leave. Kinosaki Onsen was frequented by numerous feudal lords and retainers from neighboring domains, contributing to its lively atmosphere.
[[File:kinosaki_onsen.jpg|left|150px|thumb|Postcard from Meiji 43 (1910)]]
During the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|ja|日露戦争}}, a convalescent home for wounded soldiers was established, which also ended the severe economic downturn that had persisted since the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}. In the ensuing Meiji era, many prominent literary figures—including {{ill|Naoya Shiga|ja|志賀直哉}}, who wrote {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}, and {{ill|Takeo Arishima|ja|有島武郎}}—visited Kinosaki Onsen.
Around this time, the issue of private (inner) baths became prominent. In 1925 ({{ill|Taisho Era|ja|大正}} 14), the town was completely destroyed in the {{ill|Northern Tajima Earthquake|ja|北但馬地震}}; of the approximately 1,200 bathers present, survivors fled along the tracks and were evacuated by rescue trains toward the Keihanshin region. By the following month, as many as 82 guests were already visiting Kinosaki, and as long as the hot spring flowed, the crowds never dwindled. Much of the current Japanese‑style wooden, three‑story townscape originates from the post‐earthquake reconstruction or from buildings of that era; until the earthquake, ryokan did not have private baths, and guests patronized the open‑air baths throughout the town. In 1927 ({{ill|Showa Era|ja|昭和}} 2), when {{ill|Mikiya Ryokan|ja|三木屋}} (a lodging associated with {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}) utilized a newly discovered spring on its grounds to install the first private bath in a new building, legal disputes (the “Kinosaki Onsen Private Bath Lawsuit”) erupted over the perceived breach of local tradition, lasting more than 20 years. In 1950 (Showa 25), a settlement was reached allowing private baths with regulated size, while guests desiring larger communal baths continued to use the open‑air baths. Furthermore, all hot spring sources—including those on private property—were consolidated under the former Kinosaki Town “Yushima Zaisan‑ku,” and newly drilled sources began supplying private baths. In 1972, a centralized hot water distribution management facility—akin to a municipal water supply—was constructed to deliver water via pipes to each open‑air bath and ryokan.
[[File:Nishimuraya Hotel Shogetsutei Kinosaki Onsen Japan41s3.jpg|thumb|Private Bath (Reserved {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|露天風呂|1=Rotenburo|ko|노천탕|1=Rotenburo}})]]
These reforms led to the widespread installation of private baths in ryokan; today, nearly all accommodations offer them, though even in large establishments their scale remains modest. Because guests are exempt from paying for open‑air baths, “open‑air bath tours” while clad in yukata have become a signature experience.
In 1963, the {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ}} connecting the onsen town and the summit of Daishi Mountain was opened. In step with the period of high economic growth, a hot spring boom ensued, transforming Kinosaki Onsen into a major tourist destination. In July 2008, {{ill|Kiyamachi Lane|ja|木屋町小路}} was opened on a passage linking Kiyamachi Street and {{ill|Shisho Shrine (Toyooka City)|ja|四所神社 (豊岡市)|lt=Shisho Shrine|lt_ja=四所神社}}. In January 2015, a fire broke out that resulted in two deaths and the complete loss of eight buildings ({{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Fire|ja|城崎温泉火災}}).
Toyooka DMO ({{ill|Tourism Regional Development Corporation|ja|観光地域づくり法人}}), together with young ryokan managers and Toyooka City, established the Toyooka Tourism {{ill|Digital Transformation|ja|デジタルトランスフォーメーション}} Promotion Council in 2021. This initiative shares non‑personal accommodation and reservation data to analyze where tourists originate and to forecast demand months in advance, thereby informing PR and pricing strategies.
== Management == Kinosaki Onsen is managed by the Yushima {{ill|Zaisan-ku|ja|財産区}}, which not only owns four hot spring sources and six open‑air baths but also supplies hot spring water to 84 lodging facilities (for those outside the designated area, water is delivered by {{ill|Tank Truck|ja|タンクローリー}}).<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXLASHD26H0U_W5A220C1AA1P00/ |title=外湯めぐりで共存共栄 歴史の遺物「財産区」(3) |publisher=日本経済新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref>
== Open‑Air Baths == === Seven Bath Circuit === The open‑air baths comprise the seven baths: '''{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}}''', '''{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯}}''', '''{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}}''', '''{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}}''', '''{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯}}''', '''{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯}}''', and '''{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯}}'''.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/about/spa/7onsen/ |title=城崎温泉 7つの外湯 |publisher=城崎温泉観光協会|accessdate=2022-05-21}}</ref>
<gallery> File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan03s3.jpg|{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}} – Renowned as “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation.” File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan04s3.jpg|{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯}} – The bath of the elder sister of {{ill|Emperor Gotohorikawa|ja|後堀河天皇}}, known as {{ill|Yasuka Monin|ja|邦子内親王|lt=Yasuka Monin|lt_ja=安嘉門院}}. File:Kinosaki mandarayu2816.jpg|{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}} – The bath associated with {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}}, celebrated for a thousand days of sutra recitation. File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan09s3.jpg|{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}} – Japan’s largest station building hot spring, a modern facility also featuring saunas. File:Kinosaki yanagiyu2048.jpg|{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯}} – Water that gushes forth from beneath a willow tree. File:Kinosaki jizoyu2048.jpg|{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯}} – The hot spring of the locals. File:Kinosaki konoyu1920.jpg|{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯}} – Famed for healing stork wounds. </gallery>
=== Abolition of the Ichiban‑fuda === From 2002, the former Kinosaki Town Onsen Division and the Yushima Zaisan‑ku distributed an “Ichiban‑fuda” to the first man and woman to visit the open‑air baths each day.<ref name="kobe20210327">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/sougou/202103/0014188553.shtml |title=外湯巡りの「一番札」、人気で客が奪い合い 兵庫・城崎温泉やむなく廃止へ |publisher=神戸新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref> However, its overwhelming popularity led to disputes over order and even high‑priced listings on {{ill|Mercari|ja|メルカリ}}, prompting the Yushima Zaisan‑ku to decide on its abolition at the end of March 2021.<ref name="kobe20210327"/>
Yushima Zaisan‑ku and others are now considering the planning and sale of commemorative items that can be purchased regardless of order.

== Books and Onsen == Among the noted literary figures, {{ill|Naoya Shiga|ja|志賀直哉}} stayed for {{ill|Hot Spring Treatment|ja|湯治}} due to an injury and wrote the {{ill|Short Story|ja|短編小説}} {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}. In 2013, on the centennial of Shiga’s hot spring visit, the young proprietors of various ryokan at Kinosaki Onsen established a community‑rooted publishing label called “Books and Onsen”{{efn|August 20, 2013, certified as a {{ill|Specified Nonprofit Corporation|ja|特定非営利活動法人|lt=Specified Nonprofit Corporation|lt_ja=特定非営利活動法人}} ({{Corporate Number|5140005021403}}).}}<ref>[http://books-onsen.com/ Books and Onsen] (accessed June 2018)</ref>. The first issue comprised two works by Shiga (“In Kinosaki” and its annotations); the second issue in 2014 was {{ill|Manjome Manabu|ja|万城目学|lt=Manjome Manabu|lt_ja=万城目学}}’s 『Kinosaki Trial』, and the third in 2016 was {{ill|Kanae Minato|ja|湊かなえ|lt=Kanae Minato|lt_ja=湊かなえ}}’s 『Returning to Kinosaki』. All new works, these have been released exclusively at the local ryokan. They are printed on highly water‑resistant stone paper—made not from wood {{ill|Pulp|ja|パルプ|lt=Pulp|lt_ja=パルプ}} or {{ill|Kenaf|ja|ケナフ|lt=Kenaf|lt_ja=ケナフ}}, but from an {{ill|Inorganic|ja|無機物|lt=Inorganic|lt_ja=無機物}} {{ill|Mineral|ja|鉱物|lt=Mineral|lt_ja=鉱物}} powder—with towels available as water‑repellent book covers. Additionally, the {{ill|Kinosaki Town Literary Museum|ja|城崎町文芸館}}—opened in 1996—underwent a major renovation in 2016 for its 20th anniversary.

'''Kinosaki Onsen''' (城崎温泉) is a {{ill|Hot Spring|ja|温泉}} located in {{ill|Hyogo Prefecture|ja|兵庫県}}, {{ill|Toyooka City|ja|豊岡市}}, and {{ill|Kinosaki Town|ja|城崎町}}. Possessing a long history known since before the {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代}}, it was called “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation” (海内第一泉) during the {{ill|Edo Period|ja|江戸時代}}, a claim commemorated by an extant monument. Along with {{ill|Arima Onsen|ja|有馬温泉}} and {{ill|Yumura Onsen|ja|湯村温泉 (兵庫県)|lt=Yumura Onsen|lt_ja=湯村温泉}}, it stands as one of Hyogo Prefecture’s representative hot springs.
== Water Type == * {{ill|Salt Hot Spring|ja|塩化物泉|lt=Salt Hot Spring|lt_ja=食塩泉}}: {{ill|Hot Spring Source|ja|源泉|1=Spring Mouth}} {{ill|Temperature|ja|温度}} 37 – 83 {{ill|Celsius|ja|セルシウス度|lt=Celsius|lt_ja=℃}}. All the sources are collected in a centralized hot water distribution management facility built in 1972, where the average temperature is stabilized at 57°C, and then conveyed via a network of pipes to each {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|外湯|1=sotoyu}} and {{ill|Ryokan|ja|旅館}}.
== Onsen Town == [[File:161029 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan01s.jpg|left|thumb|Nighttime Onsen Town]]
Kinosaki Onsen is a hot spring town centered on a circuit of seven open-air baths. The foremost among these, {{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}}, was originally known in the Edo period as “Arayu” (新湯), but in mid-Edo, a practitioner of the {{ill|Kohō School|ja|古方派}} of {{ill|Kampo Physician|ja|漢方医}} {{ill|Shūtoku Kagawa|ja|香川修徳|lt=Shūtoku Kagawa|lt_ja=香川修庵}} extolled its water quality and renamed it “Ichinoyu” to imply it was the best in the nation. Also, {{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}}—officially known as the Toyooka City Kinosaki Onsen Exchange Center—is managed under the designated administrator system, with its bathing and training facilities run as a public–private venture while other facilities remain municipal; its premises also house the Toyooka City Kinosaki General Branch Onsen Division. At the seven open-air baths established in the onsen town, a token called the “Ichiban-fuda” is distributed to the first bathers of the day.
An onsen town is formed along the banks of the {{ill|Daitanigawa|ja|大谿川}} (Ootani-gawa), which connects the seven open-air baths from right in front of {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|ja|城崎温泉駅}}, and along the riverbank, {{ill|Willow|ja|柳|lt=Willow|lt_ja=柳}} are planted. Lodging facilities also line the main stream of the {{ill|Maruyama River|ja|円山川}} into which the Daitanigawa flows.<ref>[http://www.kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/shop/map.html 旅館・お店情報 » マップから探す] — Kinosaki Onsen Tourism Association (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> Moreover, the group of bridges spanning the Daitanigawa was designated as an {{ill|Important Structures for Landscape Formation|ja|景観形成重要建造物等 (兵庫県指定)|lt=Important Structures for Landscape Formation|lt_ja=景観形成重要建造物}} by Hyogo Prefecture in fiscal year Heisei 18 (2006). Located near the {{ill|Sea of Japan|ja|日本海}}, the hot spring is popular for {{ill|Sea Bathing|ja|海水浴}} in summer and for {{ill|Crab|ja|カニ}} cuisine in winter. At Kinosaki Onsen Station, there is also Satono-yu (a hot spring facility within the station building) along with foot baths ({{ill|Ashiyu|ja|足湯|1=Ashiyu}}) and hot spring drinking fountains ({{ill|Hot Spring Drinking Fountain|ja|飲泉|1=Hot Spring Drinking|de|Brunnenkur|lt=drinking hot spring}}), which are scattered throughout the town.
[[File:Kinosaki Onsen01s4592.jpg|thumb|Atago Bridge]]
At Kinosaki Onsen, wearing a {{ill|Yukata|ja|浴衣}} with {{ill|Geta|ja|下駄}} is considered proper attire. As of 2007, most ryokan here provide a separate yukata for strolling the town—distinct from those used as nightwear ({{ill|Nightwear|ja|寝間着}}) within the inn. Numerous shops in the town, identifiable by a signboard reading “Yukata Advisor,” (about 30 as of 2007) offer assistance when a guest’s yukata becomes disarranged, and some {{ill|Ashitaban|ja|下足番}} even lend their geta based on the design of the yukata.
A row of wooden, three‐story ryokan lines the street, and Toyooka City applies its {{ill|Landscape Ordinance|ja|景観条例}} to protect the area.<ref>[https://www.city.toyooka.lg.jp/shisei/keikaku/toshikeikaku/1003048/1003054.html 豊岡市城崎温泉地区における歴史的建築物の保存及び活用に関する条例] (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> In 2019, the commercial facility “{{ill|Nishimura Sanpō|ja|西村屋 (城崎温泉)|lt=Nishimura Sanpō|lt_ja=さんぽう西村屋本店}},” established via a city-wide solicitation project, was designed with wooden exterior walls to harmonize with the townscape. As of 2019, there were 74 ryokan/hotels—most of which are small-scale, family-run establishments with fewer than 20 rooms—focusing on individual travelers. In 2018, approximately 630,000 tourists visited, including around 50,000 foreigners; the proportion of visitors from Europe, America, and Australia (predominantly individual travelers) was about 30%, higher than in other hot spring areas (approximately 10%). To increase the number of stays of two or more nights, comprehensive improvements to the onsen town—including its commercial facilities and the {{ill|Kinosaki International Art Center|ja|城崎国際アートセンター}}—as well as cultural initiatives such as the “Books and Onsen” project (see below) have been implemented.
Additionally, a ropeway, {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ}}, operates nearby, offering easy access to landmarks such as {{ill|Onsen Temple|ja|温泉寺 (豊岡市)|lt=Onsen Temple|lt_ja=温泉寺}}, which is revered as the guardian temple of the Kinosaki Onsen area, and to the vicinity of the summit of Daishi Mountain where an observatory is located.

== History == [[File:Kinosaki1noyu01 2816.jpg|thumb|The monument of Ichinoyu and “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation”]]
According to the {{ill|Hot Spring Founding Legend|ja|開湯伝説}}, in 629 during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Shumei|ja|舒明天皇}}, the hot spring was discovered when a {{ill|Stork|ja|コウノトリ}} was seen healing its wounds. In the early {{ill|Nara Period|ja|奈良時代}}, in 717 (the first year of the {{ill|Yōrō Era|ja|養老}}), the Buddhist monk {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}} chanted the Hachimandara Sutra for a thousand days to aid those suffering from incurable illnesses; as a result, in 720 (the fourth year of Yōrō) the sacred hot spring burst forth, marking the legendary beginning of Kinosaki Onsen. One of the seven open-air baths, {{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}}, was so named. Moreover, {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}} is also recognized as the founding priest ({{ill|Founding Priest|ja|開山 (仏教)|lt=Founding Priest|lt_ja=開山}}) of Onsen Temple, which has since become a symbol of Kinosaki Onsen.
According to the Edo‑period {{ill|Onsen Ranking|ja|温泉番付|1=Onsen rankings}}, Kinosaki Onsen was ranked in the western division’s {{ill|Sekiwaki|ja|関脇}} (with the highest rank being {{ill|Ozeki|ja|大関}}—the western Ozeki being {{ill|Arima Onsen|ja|有馬温泉}}). In that era, nine tubs served as the origin for the open‑air baths. {{ill|Kōgen Jōnin|ja|弘元上人}}, known as the “Kūkai of {{ill|Tajima Province|ja|但馬国}}” (referring to {{ill|Kūkai|ja|空海|lt=Kūkai|lt_ja=弘法大師}}) and who served as the 50th and 52nd head of {{ill|Manpuku-ji|ja|満福寺 (養父市)|lt=Manpuku-ji|lt_ja=満福寺}} in Tajima (and associated with {{ill|Mount Kōya|ja|高野山}}), was originally from the venerable ryokan {{ill|Yamamoto-ya|ja|山本屋}} of Kinosaki Onsen. During the {{ill|Bakumatsu Period|ja|幕末}}, {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|ja|木戸孝允|lt=Kido Takayoshi|lt_ja=桂小五郎}} once fled to Kinosaki Onsen while pursued by the {{ill|Shinsengumi|ja|新選組}}. In the Edo period, Kinosaki Onsen featured not only entertainment venues but also numerous food establishments offering hot pot dishes, {{ill|Zenzai|ja|ぜんざい}}, {{ill|Udon|ja|うどん}}, and {{ill|Soba|ja|蕎麦|lt=Soba|lt_ja=そば}}, while fruits, fish, and poultry were transported from afar, and even delicacies such as {{ill|Pufferfish|ja|フグ}}, {{ill|Octopus|ja|タコ}}, and {{ill|Duck|ja|鴨}} were available. Rental shops provided items including the {{ill|Shamisen|ja|三味線}}, {{ill|Sugoroku|ja|すごろく}}, {{ill|Go (board game)|ja|碁}}, {{ill|Biwa|ja|琵琶}}, and {{ill|Koto|ja|琴}}, as well as weapons like {{ill|Spear|ja|槍}} and {{ill|Sword|ja|刀}}, delighting guests so thoroughly that they would forget to leave. Kinosaki Onsen was frequented by numerous feudal lords and retainers from neighboring domains, contributing to its lively atmosphere.
[[File:kinosaki_onsen.jpg|left|150px|thumb|Postcard from Meiji 43 (1910)]]
During the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|ja|日露戦争}}, a convalescent home for wounded soldiers was established, which also ended the severe economic downturn that had persisted since the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}. In the ensuing Meiji era, many prominent literary figures—including {{ill|Naoya Shiga|ja|志賀直哉}}, who wrote {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}, and {{ill|Takeo Arishima|ja|有島武郎}}—visited Kinosaki Onsen.
Around this time, the issue of private (inner) baths became prominent. In 1925 ({{ill|Taisho Era|ja|大正}} 14), the town was completely destroyed in the {{ill|Northern Tajima Earthquake|ja|北但馬地震}}; of the approximately 1,200 bathers present, survivors fled along the tracks and were evacuated by rescue trains toward the Keihanshin region. By the following month, as many as 82 guests were already visiting Kinosaki, and as long as the hot spring flowed, the crowds never dwindled. Much of the current Japanese‑style wooden, three‑story townscape originates from the post‐earthquake reconstruction or from buildings of that era; until the earthquake, ryokan did not have private baths, and guests patronized the open‑air baths throughout the town. In 1927 ({{ill|Showa Era|ja|昭和}} 2), when {{ill|Mikiya Ryokan|ja|三木屋}} (a lodging associated with {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}) utilized a newly discovered spring on its grounds to install the first private bath in a new building, legal disputes (the “Kinosaki Onsen Private Bath Lawsuit”) erupted over the perceived breach of local tradition, lasting more than 20 years. In 1950 (Showa 25), a settlement was reached allowing private baths with regulated size, while guests desiring larger communal baths continued to use the open‑air baths. Furthermore, all hot spring sources—including those on private property—were consolidated under the former Kinosaki Town “Yushima Zaisan‑ku,” and newly drilled sources began supplying private baths. In 1972, a centralized hot water distribution management facility—akin to a municipal water supply—was constructed to deliver water via pipes to each open‑air bath and ryokan.
[[File:Nishimuraya Hotel Shogetsutei Kinosaki Onsen Japan41s3.jpg|thumb|Private Bath (Reserved {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|露天風呂|1=Rotenburo|ko|노천탕|1=Rotenburo}})]]
These reforms led to the widespread installation of private baths in ryokan; today, nearly all accommodations offer them, though even in large establishments their scale remains modest. Because guests are exempt from paying for open‑air baths, “open‑air bath tours” while clad in yukata have become a signature experience.
In 1963, the {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ}} connecting the onsen town and the summit of Daishi Mountain was opened. In step with the period of high economic growth, a hot spring boom ensued, transforming Kinosaki Onsen into a major tourist destination. In July 2008, {{ill|Kiyamachi Lane|ja|木屋町小路}} was opened on a passage linking Kiyamachi Street and {{ill|Shisho Shrine (Toyooka City)|ja|四所神社 (豊岡市)|lt=Shisho Shrine|lt_ja=四所神社}}. In January 2015, a fire broke out that resulted in two deaths and the complete loss of eight buildings ({{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Fire|ja|城崎温泉火災}}).
Toyooka DMO ({{ill|Tourism Regional Development Corporation|ja|観光地域づくり法人}}), together with young ryokan managers and Toyooka City, established the Toyooka Tourism {{ill|Digital Transformation|ja|デジタルトランスフォーメーション}} Promotion Council in 2021. This initiative shares non‑personal accommodation and reservation data to analyze where tourists originate and to forecast demand months in advance, thereby informing PR and pricing strategies.
== Management == Kinosaki Onsen is managed by the Yushima {{ill|Zaisan-ku|ja|財産区}}, which not only owns four hot spring sources and six open‑air baths but also supplies hot spring water to 84 lodging facilities (for those outside the designated area, water is delivered by {{ill|Tank Truck|ja|タンクローリー}}).<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXLASHD26H0U_W5A220C1AA1P00/ |title=外湯めぐりで共存共栄 歴史の遺物「財産区」(3) |publisher=日本経済新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref>
== Open‑Air Baths == === Seven Bath Circuit === The open‑air baths comprise the seven baths: '''{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}}''', '''{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯}}''', '''{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}}''', '''{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}}''', '''{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯}}''', '''{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯}}''', and '''{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯}}'''.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/about/spa/7onsen/ |title=城崎温泉 7つの外湯 |publisher=城崎温泉観光協会|accessdate=2022-05-21}}</ref>
<gallery> File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan03s3.jpg|{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯}} – Renowned as “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation.” File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan04s3.jpg|{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯}} – The bath of the elder sister of {{ill|Emperor Gotohorikawa|ja|後堀河天皇}}, known as {{ill|Yasuka Monin|ja|邦子内親王|lt=Yasuka Monin|lt_ja=安嘉門院}}. File:Kinosaki mandarayu2816.jpg|{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯}} – The bath associated with {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人}}, celebrated for a thousand days of sutra recitation. File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan09s3.jpg|{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯}} – Japan’s largest station building hot spring, a modern facility also featuring saunas. File:Kinosaki yanagiyu2048.jpg|{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯}} – Water that gushes forth from beneath a willow tree. File:Kinosaki jizoyu2048.jpg|{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯}} – The hot spring of the locals. File:Kinosaki konoyu1920.jpg|{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯}} – Famed for healing stork wounds. </gallery>
=== Abolition of the Ichiban‑fuda === From 2002, the former Kinosaki Town Onsen Division and the Yushima Zaisan‑ku distributed an “Ichiban‑fuda” to the first man and woman to visit the open‑air baths each day.<ref name="kobe20210327">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/sougou/202103/0014188553.shtml |title=外湯巡りの「一番札」、人気で客が奪い合い 兵庫・城崎温泉やむなく廃止へ |publisher=神戸新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref> However, its overwhelming popularity led to disputes over order and even high‑priced listings on {{ill|Mercari|ja|メルカリ}}, prompting the Yushima Zaisan‑ku to decide on its abolition at the end of March 2021.<ref name="kobe20210327"/>
Yushima Zaisan‑ku and others are now considering the planning and sale of commemorative items that can be purchased regardless of order.
== Festivals and Events == * {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Summer Story|ja|城崎温泉夏物語}} – A summer festival held from late July to late August. ** Kinosaki Onsen Yukemuri {{ill|Taiko Drums|ja|太鼓}} ** Kinosaki {{ill|Lantern Floating|ja|灯篭流し}} – Late August ** Kinosaki Onsen Hometown Festival {{ill|Fireworks|ja|花火}} Competition, “Yume Hanabi” – Late August
== Tourism == === Landmarks === * Temples and Shrines – {{ill|Onsen Temple|ja|温泉寺 (豊岡市)|lt=Onsen Temple|lt_ja=温泉寺}}, {{ill|Shisho Shrine (Toyooka City)|ja|四所神社 (豊岡市)|lt=Shisho Shrine|lt_ja=四所神社}}, and {{ill|Gokuraku-ji|ja|極楽寺 (豊岡市)|lt=Gokuraku-ji|lt_ja=極楽寺}}. * Museums – {{ill|Kinosaki Art Museum|ja|城崎美術館}}, {{ill|Kinosaki Literary Museum|ja|城崎文芸館}}, {{ill|Otagaki Shiro Museum|ja|太田垣士郎資料館}}, and {{ill|Kinosaki Straw Craft Heritage Museum|ja|城崎麦わら細工伝承館}}. <gallery> File:Onsenji05 2048.jpg|{{ill|Onsen Temple (Toyooka City)|ja|温泉寺 (豊岡市)|lt=Onsen Temple|lt_ja=温泉寺}} File:Gokurakuji Toyooka Hyogo pref Japan01s3.jpg|{{ill|Gokuraku-ji (Toyooka City)|ja|極楽寺 (豊岡市)|lt=Gokuraku-ji|lt_ja=極楽寺}} File:Kinosaki mugiwara2048.jpg|{{ill|Kinosaki Straw Craft Heritage Museum|ja|城崎麦わら細工伝承館|lt=Kinosaki Straw Craft Heritage Museum|lt_ja=城崎麦わら細工伝承館}} File:Kinosaki museum02 2816.jpg|{{ill|Kinosaki Art Museum|ja|城崎美術館|lt=Kinosaki Art Museum|lt_ja=城崎美術館}} File:Kinosaki bungei01 2816.jpg|{{ill|Kinosaki Literary Museum|ja|城崎文芸館|lt=Kinosaki Literary Museum|lt_ja=城崎文芸館}} – Housing works related to the history of Kinosaki and literary figures associated with it. File:Kinosaki ropeway01n2610.jpg|{{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ|lt=Kinosaki Ropeway|lt_ja=城崎ロープウェイ}} </gallery>

== Notable People Associated with Kinosaki Onsen == === Notable People from Kinosaki Onsen === * {{ill|Kōgen Jōnin|ja|弘元上人}} (known as the “Kūkai of {{ill|Tajima Province|ja|但馬国}}”) === Residents of Kinosaki Onsen === * {{ill|Hiura Satoru|ja|ひうらさとる}} (manga artist) === Notable Visitors to Kinosaki Onsen === {{ill|Arishima Takeo|ja|有島武郎|lt=Arishima Takeo|lt_ja=有島武郎}}, {{ill|Kyoka Izumi|ja|泉鏡花}}, {{ill|Keikyoku Kiyoh|ja|京極杞陽}}, {{ill|Kenko Hōshi|ja|卜部兼好|lt=Kenko Hōshi|lt_ja=兼好法師}}, {{ill|Mokichi Saitō|ja|斎藤茂吉}}, {{ill|Naoya Shiga|ja|志賀直哉}}, {{ill|Shōgo Hakuchō|ja|白鳥省吾}}, {{ill|Kuriyama Shibano|ja|柴野栗山}}, {{ill|Ryotaro Shiba|ja|司馬遼太郎}}, {{ill|Tōson Shimazaki|ja|島崎藤村}}, {{ill|Zōan Sōhō|ja|沢庵宗彭|lt=Zōan|lt_ja=沢庵}}, {{ill|Fuyuhiko Tanaka|ja|田中冬二}}, {{ill|Sohō Tokutomi|ja|徳富蘇峰}}, {{ill|Seishi Yamaguchi|ja|山口誓子}}, {{ill|Isamu Yoshii|ja|吉井勇}}, {{ill|Tokutomi Roka|ja|徳富蘦花}}, {{ill|Saika Tomita|ja|富田砕花}}, {{ill|Kusajo Hino|ja|日野草城}}, {{ill|Kensuke Fujiwara|ja|藤原兼輔}}, {{ill|Samio Maekawa|ja|前川佐美雄}}, {{ill|Kurai Mukai|ja|向井去来}}, {{ill|Kunio Yanagida|ja|柳田國男}}, {{ill|Akiko Yosano|ja|与謝野晶子}}, and {{ill|Tekkkan Yosano|ja|与謝野鉄幹}}.
== Local Characters == * {{ill|Matsuba Crab|ja|松葉カニ|lt=Matsuba Crab|lt_ja=松葉カニ}}: Joe (younger brother) and Saki (older sister) * {{ill|Stork|ja|コウノトリ|lt=Stork|lt_ja=コウノトリ}}: Shō-kun and Mai-chan (a couple) * {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Senchitai Onsenja|ja|城崎泉隊オンセンジャー|lt=Kinosaki Onsen Senchitai Onsenja|lt_ja=城崎泉隊オンセンジャー}} (Sotoy Red, Yukata Blue, Mugi Wry Yellow) * The evil organization Hedarark (General Kigawaru, the Bath Tub Monster Skahn, the Prankster Koujagero, Chokkai)
== Books and Onsen == Among the noted literary figures, {{ill|Naoya Shiga|ja|志賀直哉}} stayed for {{ill|Hot Spring Treatment|ja|湯治}} due to an injury and wrote the {{ill|Short Story|ja|短編小説}} {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて}}. In 2013, on the centennial of Shiga’s hot spring visit, the young proprietors of various ryokan at Kinosaki Onsen established a community‑rooted publishing label called “Books and Onsen”{{efn|August 20, 2013, certified as a {{ill|Specified Nonprofit Corporation|ja|特定非営利活動法人|lt=Specified Nonprofit Corporation|lt_ja=特定非営利活動法人}} ({{Corporate Number|5140005021403}}).}}<ref>[http://books-onsen.com/ Books and Onsen] (accessed June 2018)</ref>. The first issue comprised two works by Shiga (“In Kinosaki” and its annotations); the second issue in 2014 was {{ill|Manjome Manabu|ja|万城目学|lt=Manjome Manabu|lt_ja=万城目学}}’s 『Kinosaki Trial』, and the third in 2016 was {{ill|Kanae Minato|ja|湊かなえ|lt=Kanae Minato|lt_ja=湊かなえ}}’s 『Returning to Kinosaki』. All new works, these have been released exclusively at the local ryokan. They are printed on highly water‑resistant stone paper—made not from wood {{ill|Pulp|ja|パルプ|lt=Pulp|lt_ja=パルプ}} or {{ill|Kenaf|ja|ケナフ|lt=Kenaf|lt_ja=ケナフ}}, but from an {{ill|Inorganic|ja|無機物|lt=Inorganic|lt_ja=無機物}} {{ill|Mineral|ja|鉱物|lt=Mineral|lt_ja=鉱物}} powder—with towels available as water‑repellent book covers. Additionally, the {{ill|Kinosaki Town Literary Museum|ja|城崎町文芸館}}—opened in 1996—underwent a major renovation in 2016 for its 20th anniversary.
== Access == ; Railway * On the {{ill|Sanin Main Line|ja|山陰本線|lt=Sanin Main Line|lt_ja=山陰本線}} ({{ill|JR West|ja|西日本旅客鉄道|lt=JR West|lt_ja=JR西日本}}), alight immediately at {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|ja|城崎温泉駅|lt=Kinosaki Onsen Station|lt_ja=城崎温泉駅}}. ; Bus * From {{ill|Kyoto Station|ja|京都駅|lt=Kyoto Station|lt_ja=京都駅}}, {{ill|Osaka City|ja|大阪市|lt=Osaka City|lt_ja=大阪市}} (via {{ill|Hankyu Sanbancho Express Bus Terminal|ja|阪急三番街高速バスターミナル|lt=Hankyu Sanbancho Express Bus Terminal|lt_ja=阪急三番街高速バスターミナル}}), and {{ill|Kobe City|ja|神戸市|lt=Kobe City|lt_ja=神戸市}} (via {{ill|Sannomiya Station Bus Stop|ja|三宮駅バスのりば#神姫バス神戸三宮バスターミナル|lt=Sannomiya Station Bus Stop|lt_ja=三宮駅バスのりば}}), take the {{ill|Zentan Express Bus|ja|全但特急バス|lt=Zentan Express Bus|lt_ja=全但特急バス}} to get off at either {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|ja|城崎温泉駅|lt=Kinosaki Onsen Station|lt_ja=城崎温泉駅}} or “Kinosaki Onsen”. ; Airplane : {{ill|Tokyo International Airport|ja|東京国際空港|lt=Tokyo International Airport|lt_ja=東京国際空港}} ({{ill|Haneda Airport|ja|羽田空港|lt=Haneda Airport|lt_ja=羽田空港}}) ← ({{ill|Japan Airlines|ja|日本航空|lt=Japan Airlines|lt_ja=日本航空}}) → {{ill|Osaka International Airport|ja|大阪国際空港|lt=Osaka International Airport|lt_ja=大阪国際空港}} ({{ill|Itami Airport|ja|伊丹空港|lt=Itami Airport|lt_ja=伊丹空港}}) ← ({{ill|Japan Air Commuter|ja|日本エアコミューター|lt=Japan Air Commuter|lt_ja=日本エアコミューター}}) → {{ill|Kōnotori Tajima Airport|ja|コウノトリ但馬空港|lt=Kōnotori Tajima Airport|lt_ja=コウノトリ但馬空港}}<br/> Kōnotori Tajima service is linked with the Japan Airlines Tokyo flight. From Kōnotori Tajima Airport, it is a 40‑minute ride by airport bus to Kinosaki Onsen. ; Private Car * {{Ja Exp Route Sign|E27}}{{ill|Maizuru Wakasa Expressway|ja|舞鶴若狭自動車道|lt=Maizuru Wakasa Expressway|lt_ja=舞鶴若狭自動車道}} at {{ill|Kasuga Interchange|ja|春日インターチェンジ|lt=Kasuga Interchange|lt_ja=春日インターチェンジ}}, via the {{ill|Hokkin-Kinki Toyooka Expressway|ja|北近畿豊岡自動車道|lt=Hokkin-Kinki Toyooka Expressway|lt_ja=北近畿豊岡自動車道}}, {{ill|National Route 312|ja|国道312号|lt=National Route 312|lt_ja=国道312号}}, and {{ill|Hyogo Prefectural Route 3 Toyooka Seto Line|ja|兵庫県道3号豊岡瀬戸線|lt=Hyogo Prefectural Route 3 Toyooka Seto Line|lt_ja=兵庫県道3号豊岡瀬戸線}}, etc.
