'''Kinosaki Onsen''' (城崎温泉) is a {{ill|Onsen|en|Onsen|WD=Q655311|lt=Onsen}} located in {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture}}, {{ill|Toyooka, Hyōgo|en|Toyooka, Hyōgo|WD=Q696388|lt=Toyooka City}}, and {{ill|Kinosaki, Hyōgo|en|Kinosaki, Hyōgo|WD=Q6414198|lt=Kinosaki Town}}. Possessing a long history known since before the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian Period}}, it was called “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation” (海内第一泉) during the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo Period}}, a claim commemorated by an extant monument. Along with {{ill|Arima Onsen|en|Arima Onsen|WD=Q4790673|lt=Arima Onsen}} and {{ill|Yumura Onsen (Hyogo)|en|Yumura Onsen (Hyogo)|WD=Q8061163|lt=Yumura Onsen}}, it stands as one of Hyōgo Prefecture’s representative hot springs.
== Water Type == * {{ill|Brine spring|en|Brine spring|WD=Q11428612|lt=Salt Hot Spring}}: {{ill|Hot Spring Source|ja|源泉|1=Spring Mouth|1=Spring Mouth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Source|13=User:Immanuelle/Spring Mouth|qq=}} {{ill|Temperature|en|Temperature|WD=Q11466|lt=Temperature}} 37 – 83 {{ill|Celsius|en|Celsius|WD=Q25267|lt=Celsius}}. All the sources are collected in a centralized hot water distribution management facility built in 1972, where the average temperature is stabilized at 57°C, and then conveyed via a network of pipes to each {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|外湯|1=Sotoyu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Open-Air Bath|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotoyu|qq=}} and {{ill|Ryokan|en|Ryokan|WD=Q562930|lt=Ryokan}}.
== Onsen Town == [[File:161029 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan01s.jpg|left|thumb|Nighttime Onsen Town]]
Kinosaki Onsen is a hot spring town centered on a circuit of seven open-air baths. The foremost among these, {{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinoyu|1=Ichinoyu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17988814}}, was originally known in the Edo period as “Arayu” (新湯), but in mid-Edo, a practitioner of the {{ill|Kohō School|ja|古方派|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kohō School|1=Kohō school|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10913345}} of {{ill|Kampo Physician|ja|漢方医|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kampo Physician|1=Kampo physician|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11565521}} {{ill|Shūtoku Kagawa|ja|香川修徳|lt=Shūtoku Kagawa|lt_ja=香川修庵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shūtoku Kagawa|1=Kagawa Shūtoku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q6561882}} extolled its water quality and renamed it “Ichinoyu” to imply it was the best in the nation. Also, {{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satono-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540739}}—officially known as the Toyooka City Kinosaki Onsen Exchange Center—is managed under the designated administrator system, with its bathing and training facilities run as a public–private venture while other facilities remain municipal; its premises also house the Toyooka City Kinosaki General Branch Onsen Division. At the seven open-air baths established in the onsen town, a token called the “Ichiban-fuda” is distributed to the first bathers of the day.
An onsen town is formed along the banks of the {{ill|Daitanigawa|ja|大谿川|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daitanigawa|1=Ōtani River|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11439183}} (Ootani-gawa), which connects the seven open-air baths from right in front of {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|en|Kinosaki Onsen Station|WD=Q1055689|lt=Kinosaki Onsen Station}}, and along the riverbank, {{ill|Willow|ja|柳|lt=Willow|lt_ja=柳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Willow|1=柳|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15884500}} are planted. Lodging facilities also line the main stream of the {{ill|Maruyama River|en|Maruyama River|WD=Q11394765|lt=Maruyama River}} into which the Daitanigawa flows.<ref>[http://www.kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/shop/map.html 旅館・お店情報 » マップから探す] — Kinosaki Onsen Tourism Association (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> Moreover, the group of bridges spanning the Daitanigawa was designated as an {{ill|Important Structures for Landscape Formation|ja|景観形成重要建造物等 (兵庫県指定)|lt=Important Structures for Landscape Formation|lt_ja=景観形成重要建造物|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Important Structures for Landscape Formation|1=Important Structures for Landscape Formation|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514688}} by Hyōgo Prefecture in fiscal year Heisei 18 (2006). Located near the {{ill|Sea of Japan|en|Sea of Japan|WD=Q27092|lt=Sea of Japan}}, the hot spring is popular for {{ill|Sea bathing|en|Sea bathing|WD=Q1132965|lt=Sea Bathing}} in summer and for {{ill|Crab|en|Crab|WD=Q16033394|lt=Crab}} cuisine in winter. At Kinosaki Onsen Station, there is also Satono-yu (a hot spring facility within the station building) along with foot baths ({{ill|Ashiyu|en|Ashiyu|WD=Q725522|lt=Ashiyu}}) and hot spring drinking fountains ({{ill|Hot Spring Drinking Fountain|ja|飲泉|1=Hot Spring Drinking|de|Brunnenkur|lt=drinking hot spring|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Drinking Fountain|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Drinking|qq=}}), which are scattered throughout the town.
[[File:Kinosaki Onsen01s4592.jpg|thumb|Atago Bridge]]
At Kinosaki Onsen, wearing a {{ill|Yukata|en|Yukata|WD=Q849302|lt=Yukata}} with {{ill|Geta (footwear)|en|Geta (footwear)|WD=Q721941|lt=Geta}} is considered proper attire. As of 2007, most ryokan here provide a separate yukata for strolling the town—distinct from those used as nightwear ({{ill|Nightwear|ja|寝間着|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nightwear|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 寝巻|1=nightwear|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1187616}}) within the inn. Numerous shops in the town, identifiable by a signboard reading “Yukata Advisor,” (about 30 as of 2007) offer assistance when a guest’s yukata becomes disarranged, and some {{ill|Ashitaban|ja|下足番|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ashitaban|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 下駄箱|1=getabako|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2855743}} even lend their geta based on the design of the yukata.
A row of wooden, three‐story ryokan lines the street, and Toyooka City applies its {{ill|Landscape Ordinance|ja|景観条例|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Landscape Ordinance|1=Regulations of cityscape (in Japan)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514689}} to protect the area.<ref>[https://www.city.toyooka.lg.jp/shisei/keikaku/toshikeikaku/1003048/1003054.html 豊岡市城崎温泉地区における歴史的建築物の保存及び活用に関する条例] (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> In 2019, the commercial facility “{{ill|Nishimura Sanpō|ja|西村屋 (城崎温泉)|lt=Nishimura Sanpō|lt_ja=さんぽう西村屋本店|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nishimura Sanpō|1=Nishimuraya|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q105552895}},” established via a city-wide solicitation project, was designed with wooden exterior walls to harmonize with the townscape. As of 2019, there were 74 ryokan/hotels—most of which are small-scale, family-run establishments with fewer than 20 rooms—focusing on individual travelers. In 2018, approximately 630,000 tourists visited, including around 50,000 foreigners; the proportion of visitors from Europe, America, and Australia (predominantly individual travelers) was about 30%, higher than in other hot spring areas (approximately 10%). To increase the number of stays of two or more nights, comprehensive improvements to the onsen town—including its commercial facilities and the {{ill|Kinosaki International Art Center|ja|城崎国際アートセンター|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki International Art Center|1=Kinosaki International Arts Center|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q21652936}}—as well as cultural initiatives such as the “Books and Onsen” project (see below) have been implemented.
Additionally, a ropeway, {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Ropeway|1=Kinosaki Ropeway|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11426138}}, operates nearby, offering easy access to landmarks such as {{ill|Onsen Temple|ja|温泉寺 (豊岡市)|lt=Onsen Temple|lt_ja=温泉寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Temple|qq=}}, which is revered as the guardian temple of the Kinosaki Onsen area, and to the vicinity of the summit of Daishi Mountain where an observatory is located.
<gallery widths="160px" heights="110px"> Kinosaki onsen04 1920.jpg|Overview of the Onsen Town 一番札.jpg|Ichiban‑fuda 100722 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan03s3.jpg|Station Street Kinosaki onsen01 2816.jpg|Yunosato Street (the front right is “{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gyosho-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}”) </gallery>
== History == [[File:Kinosaki1noyu01 2816.jpg|thumb|The monument of Ichinoyu and “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation”]]
According to the {{ill|Hot Spring Founding Legend|ja|開湯伝説|1=Onsen Origin Myth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Founding Legend|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Origin Myth|qq=}}, in 629 during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|en|Emperor Jomei|WD=Q329761|lt=Emperor Shumei}}, the hot spring was discovered when a {{ill|Oriental stork|en|Oriental stork|WD=Q998495|lt=Stork}} was seen healing its wounds. In the early {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara Period}}, in 717 (the first year of the {{ill|Yōrō|en|Yōrō|WD=Q1373061|lt=Yōrō Era}}), the Buddhist monk {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōchi Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} chanted the Hachimandara Sutra for a thousand days to aid those suffering from incurable illnesses; as a result, in 720 (the fourth year of Yōrō) the sacred hot spring burst forth, marking the legendary beginning of Kinosaki Onsen. One of the seven open-air baths, {{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mandarayu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540745}}, was so named. Moreover, {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōchi Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} is also recognized as the founding priest ({{ill|Kaisan|en|Kaisan|WD=Q3191999|lt=Founding Priest}}) of Onsen Temple, which has since become a symbol of Kinosaki Onsen.
According to the Edo‑period {{ill|Onsen Ranking|ja|温泉番付|1=onsen banzuke|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Ranking|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Rankings|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11562960}}, Kinosaki Onsen was Ranked in the western division’s {{ill|Sekiwaki|ja|関脇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sekiwaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=sekiwake|WD=Q1937166}} (with the highest Rank being {{ill|Ozeki|ja|大関|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ozeki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=ōzeki|WD=Q2166602}}—the western Ozeki being {{ill|Arima Onsen|en|Arima Onsen|WD=Q4790673|lt=Arima Onsen}}). In that era, nine tubs served as the origin for the open‑air baths. {{ill|Kōgen Jōnin|ja|弘元上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōgen Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弘元|1=Kōgen Jōnin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q45830120}}, known as the “Kūkai of {{ill|Tajima Province|en|Tajima Province|WD=Q1053727|lt=Tajima Province}}” (referring to {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}}) and who served as the 50th and 52nd head of {{ill|Manpuku-ji|ja|満福寺 (養父市)|lt=Manpuku-ji|lt_ja=満福寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manpuku-ji|qq=}} in Tajima (and associated with {{ill|Mount Kōya|en|Mount Kōya|WD=Q535065|lt=Mount Kōya}}), was originally from the venerable ryokan {{ill|Yamamoto-ya|ja|山本屋|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamamoto-ya|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Kinosaki Onsen. During the {{ill|Bakumatsu|en|Bakumatsu|WD=Q804558|lt=Bakumatsu Period}}, {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|en|Kido Takayoshi|WD=Q696402|lt=Kido Takayoshi}} once fled to Kinosaki Onsen while pursued by the {{ill|Shinsengumi|en|Shinsengumi|WD=Q221031|lt=Shinsengumi}}. In the Edo period, Kinosaki Onsen featured not only entertainment venues but also numerous food establishments offering hot pot dishes, {{ill|Zenzai|ja|ぜんざい|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zenzai|1=zenzai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11270244}}, {{ill|Udon|en|Udon|WD=Q471861|lt=Udon}}, and {{ill|Soba|en|Soba|WD=Q753910|lt=Soba}}, while fruits, fish, and poultry were transported from afar, and even delicacies such as {{ill|Fugu|en|Fugu|WD=Q134385|lt=Pufferfish}}, {{ill|Octopus|en|Octopus|WD=Q40152|lt=Octopus}}, and {{ill|Duck|ja|鴨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Duck|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to カモ|1=duck|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3736439}} were available. Rental shops provided items including the {{ill|Shamisen|en|Shamisen|WD=Q241337|lt=Shamisen}}, {{ill|Sugoroku|en|Sugoroku|WD=Q1472906|lt=Sugoroku}}, {{ill|Go (board game)|ja|碁|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Go (board game)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 囲碁|1=go|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11413}}, {{ill|Biwa|ja|琵琶|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Biwa|1=pipa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q6685124}}, and {{ill|Koto|ja|琴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Koto|1=kin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11086494}}, as well as weapons like {{ill|Spear|en|Spear|WD=Q44475|lt=Spear}} and {{ill|Single-edged sword|en|Single-edged sword|WD=Q7523706|lt=Sword}}, delighting guests so thoroughly that they would forget to leave. Kinosaki Onsen was frequented by numerous feudal lords and retainers from neighboring domains, contributing to its lively atmosphere.
[[File:kinosaki_onsen.jpg|left|150px|thumb|Postcard from Meiji 43 (1910)]]
During the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|WD=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War}}, a convalescent home for wounded soldiers was established, which also ended the severe economic downturn that had persisted since the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|en|Meiji Restoration|WD=Q8707|lt=Meiji Restoration}}. In the ensuing Meiji era, many prominent literary figures—including {{ill|Naoya Shiga|en|Naoya Shiga|WD=Q957997|lt=Naoya Shiga}}, who wrote {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/In Kinosaki|1=At Kinosaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11425921}}, and {{ill|Takeo Arishima|en|Takeo Arishima|WD=Q577180|lt=Takeo Arishima}}—visited Kinosaki Onsen.
Around this time, the issue of private (inner) baths became prominent. In 1925 ({{ill|Taishō era|en|Taishō era|WD=Q329174|lt=Taisho Era}} 14), the town was completely destroyed in the {{ill|1925 North Tajima earthquake|en|1925 North Tajima earthquake|WD=Q11401118|lt=Northern Tajima Earthquake}}; of the approximately 1,200 bathers present, survivors fled along the tracks and were evacuated by rescue trains toward the Keihanshin region. By the following month, as many as 82 guests were already visiting Kinosaki, and as long as the hot spring flowed, the crowds never dwindled. Much of the current Japanese‑style wooden, three‑story townscape originates from the post‐earthquake reconstruction or from buildings of that era; until the earthquake, ryokan did not have private baths, and guests patronized the open‑air baths throughout the town. In 1927 ({{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Showa Era}} 2), when {{ill|Mikiya Ryokan|ja|三木屋|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikiya Ryokan|1=Mikiya|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q55533899}} (a lodging associated with {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/In Kinosaki|1=At Kinosaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11425921}}) utilized a newly discovered spring on its grounds to install the first private bath in a new building, legal disputes (the “Kinosaki Onsen Private Bath Lawsuit”) erupted over the perceived breach of local tradition, lasting more than 20 years. In 1950 (Showa 25), a settlement was reached allowing private baths with regulated size, while guests desiring larger communal baths continued to use the open‑air baths. Furthermore, all hot spring sources—including those on private property—were consolidated under the former Kinosaki Town “Yushima Zaisan‑ku,” and newly drilled sources began supplying private baths. In 1972, a centralized hot water distribution management facility—akin to a municipal water supply—was constructed to deliver water via pipes to each open‑air bath and ryokan.
[[File:Nishimuraya Hotel Shogetsutei Kinosaki Onsen Japan41s3.jpg|thumb|Private Bath (Reserved {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|露天風呂|1=Outdoor hot spring baths|1=Outdoor hot spring baths|ko|노천탕|1=Outdoor hot spring baths|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Open-Air Bath|13=User:Immanuelle/Outdoor hot spring baths|qq=}})]]
These reforms led to the widespread installation of private baths in ryokan; today, nearly all accommodations offer them, though even in large establishments their scale remains modest. Because guests are exempt from paying for open‑air baths, “open‑air bath tours” while clad in yukata have become a signature experience.
In 1963, the {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Ropeway|1=Kinosaki Ropeway|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11426138}} connecting the onsen town and the summit of Daishi Mountain was opened. In step with the period of high economic growth, a hot spring boom ensued, transforming Kinosaki Onsen into a major tourist destination. In July 2008, {{ill|Kiyamachi Lane|ja|木屋町小路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiyamachi Lane|1=Kiyamachi Kōji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11518305}} was opened on a passage linking Kiyamachi Street and {{ill|Shisho Shrine (Toyooka)|ja|四所神社 (豊岡市)|lt=Shisho Shrine|lt_ja=四所神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shisho Shrine (Toyooka City)|qq=}}. In January 2015, a fire broke out that resulted in two deaths and the complete loss of eight buildings ({{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Fire|ja|城崎温泉火災|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Onsen Fire|1=Kinosaki Onsen Fire|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24862932}}).
Toyooka DMO ({{ill|Destination marketing organization|en|Destination marketing organization|WD=Q3689421|lt=Tourism Regional Development Corporation}}), together with young ryokan managers and Toyooka City, established the Toyooka Tourism {{ill|Digital transformation|en|Digital transformation|WD=Q4252370|lt=Digital Transformation}} Promotion Council in 2021. This initiative shares non‑personal accommodation and reservation data to analyze where tourists originate and to forecast demand months in advance, thereby informing PR and pricing strategies.
== Management == Kinosaki Onsen is managed by the Yushima {{ill|Zaisan-ku|ja|財産区|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zaisan-ku|1=property ward|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q55521203}}, which not only owns four hot spring sources and six open‑air baths but also supplies hot spring water to 84 lodging facilities (for those outside the designated area, water is delivered by {{ill|Tank truck|en|Tank truck|WD=Q20465|lt=Tank Truck}}).<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXLASHD26H0U_W5A220C1AA1P00/ |title=外湯めぐりで共存共栄 歴史の遺物「財産区」(3) |publisher=日本経済新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref>
== Open‑Air Baths == === Seven Bath Circuit === The open‑air baths comprise the seven baths: '''{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinoyu|1=Ichinoyu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17988814}}''', '''{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gyosho-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540751}}''', '''{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mandarayu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540745}}''', '''{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satono-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540739}}''', '''{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yanagiyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540756}}''', '''{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jizoyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''', and '''{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Konoyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540761}}'''.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/about/spa/7onsen/ |title=城崎温泉 7つの外湯 |publisher=城崎温泉観光協会|accessdate=2022-05-21}}</ref>
<gallery> File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan03s3.jpg|{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinoyu|qq=}} – Renowned as “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation.” File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan04s3.jpg|{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gyosho-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – The bath of the elder sister of {{ill|Emperor Go-Horikawa|en|Emperor Go-Horikawa|WD=Q357221|lt=Emperor Gotohorikawa}}, known as {{ill|Princess Kuniko|en|Princess Kuniko|WD=Q6145785|lt=Yasuka Monin}}. File:Kinosaki mandarayu2816.jpg|{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mandarayu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – The bath associated with {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōchi Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, celebrated for a thousand days of sutra recitation. File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan09s3.jpg|{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satono-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – Japan’s largest station building hot spring, a modern facility also featuring saunas. File:Kinosaki yanagiyu2048.jpg|{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yanagiyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – Water that gushes forth from beneath a willow tree. File:Kinosaki jizoyu2048.jpg|{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jizoyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – The hot spring of the locals. File:Kinosaki konoyu1920.jpg|{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Konoyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – Famed for healing stork wounds. </gallery>
=== Abolition of the Ichiban‑fuda === From 2002, the former Kinosaki Town Onsen Division and the Yushima Zaisan‑ku distributed an “Ichiban‑fuda” to the first man and woman to visit the open‑air baths each day.<ref name="kobe20210327">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/sougou/202103/0014188553.shtml |title=外湯巡りの「一番札」、人気で客が奪い合い 兵庫・城崎温泉やむなく廃止へ |publisher=神戸新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref> However, its overwhelming popularity led to disputes over order and even high‑priced listings on {{ill|Mercari|en|Mercari|WD=Q21019721|lt=Mercari}}, prompting the Yushima Zaisan‑ku to decide on its abolition at the end of March 2021.<ref name="kobe20210327"/>
Yushima Zaisan‑ku and others are now considering the planning and sale of commemorative items that can be purchased regardless of order.

== Books and Onsen == Among the noted literary figures, {{ill|Naoya Shiga|en|Naoya Shiga|WD=Q957997|lt=Naoya Shiga}} stayed for {{ill|Hot Spring Treatment|ja|湯治|1=thermal bath|2=ja|3=湯治|4=zh|5=湯治|6=ca|7=Termalisme|8=de|9=Thermalbad|10=es|11=Termalismo|13=Thermal bath|14=eo|15=Varmfonta banejo|16=fr|17=Thermalisme|18=la|19=Balneum thermale|20=lb|21=Thermalbad|22=hu|23=Termálfürdő|24=nl|25=Thermaalbad|26=pt|27=Turismo termal|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Treatment|13=User:Immanuelle/Thermal bath|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1004887}} due to an injury and wrote the {{ill|Short story|en|Short story|WD=Q49084|lt=Short Story}} {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/In Kinosaki|1=At Kinosaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11425921}}. In 2013, on the centennial of Shiga’s hot spring visit, the young proprietors of various ryokan at Kinosaki Onsen established a community‑rooted publishing label called “Books and Onsen”{{efn|August 20, 2013, certified as a {{ill|Specified Nonprofit Corporation|ja|特定非営利活動法人|lt=Specified Nonprofit Corporation|lt_ja=特定非営利活動法人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Specified Nonprofit Corporation|1=specified non-profit corporation|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11570934}} ({{Corporate Number|5140005021403}}).}}<ref>[http://books-onsen.com/ Books and Onsen] (accessed June 2018)</ref>. The first issue comprised two works by Shiga (“In Kinosaki” and its annotations); the second issue in 2014 was {{ill|Manjome Manabu|ja|万城目学|lt=Manjome Manabu|lt_ja=万城目学|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manjome Manabu|1=Manabu Makime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q9004033}}’s 『Kinosaki Trial』, and the third in 2016 was {{ill|Kanae Minato|en|Kanae Minato|WD=Q4390332|lt=Kanae Minato}}’s 『Returning to Kinosaki』. All new works, these have been released exclusively at the local ryokan. They are printed on highly water‑resistant stone paper—made not from wood {{ill|Pulp (paper)|en|Pulp (paper)|WD=Q672506|lt=Pulp}} or {{ill|Kenaf|en|Kenaf|WD=Q1137540|lt=Kenaf}}, but from an {{ill|Inorganic|ja|無機物|lt=Inorganic|lt_ja=無機物|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inorganic|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 無機化合物|1=inorganic compound|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q190065}} {{ill|Mineral|en|Mineral|WD=Q7946|lt=Mineral}} powder—with towels available as water‑repellent book covers. Additionally, the {{ill|Kinosaki Town Literary Museum|ja|城崎町文芸館|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Town Literary Museum|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 城崎文芸館|1=Kinosaki Bungeikan Heritage Museum|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11426143}}—opened in 1996—underwent a major renovation in 2016 for its 20th anniversary.

{{infobox Onsen |Name = Kinosaki Onsen |image = Kinosaki onsen02 1920.jpg |Comment = The hot spring town is traversed by the {{ill|Daitanigawa|ja|大谿川|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daitanigawa|1=Ōtani River|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11439183}} |Location = {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture}} {{ill|Toyooka, Hyōgo|en|Toyooka, Hyōgo|WD=Q696388|lt=Toyooka City}} {{ill|Kinosaki, Hyōgo|en|Kinosaki, Hyōgo|WD=Q6414198|lt=Kinosaki Town}} |Coordinates = {{Wiki Coordinates Two-Stage DMS|35|37|40|N|134|48|0|E|type:landmark_region:JP-28|display=inline,title}} |Access = * Railway: {{ill|West Japan Railway Company|en|West Japan Railway Company|WD=Q502125|lt=JR}} {{ill|San'in Main Line|en|San'in Main Line|WD=Q1135170|lt=Sanin Main Line}} – alight immediately at {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|en|Kinosaki Onsen Station|WD=Q1055689|lt=Kinosaki Onsen Station}} * Highway Bus: From {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|WD=Q35765|lt=Osaka City}} and {{ill|Kobe|en|Kobe|WD=Q48320|lt=Kobe City}}, take the {{ill|Zentan Express Bus|ja|全但バス|lt=Zentan Express Bus|lt_ja=全但特急バス|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zentan Express Bus|1=Zentan Bus|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11389110}} to {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|en|Kinosaki Onsen Station|WD=Q1055689|lt=Kinosaki Onsen Station}} or get off at “Kinosaki Onsen” * Airplane: From {{ill|Itami Airport|en|Itami Airport|WD=Q1046748|lt=Osaka International Airport}}, 30 minutes to {{ill|Tajima Airport|ja|但馬空港|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tajima Airport|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 但馬飛行場|1=Tajima Airport|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1931194}}, then 40 minutes by {{ill|Zentan Express Bus|ja|全但バス|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zentan Express Bus|1=Zentan Bus|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11389110}} |Water Type = {{ill|Brine spring|en|Brine spring|WD=Q11428612|lt=Brine spring}} |Temperature = 37 - '''Kinosaki Onsen''' (城崎温泉) is a {{ill|Onsen|en|Onsen|WD=Q655311|lt=Onsen}} located in {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture}}, {{ill|Toyooka, Hyōgo|en|Toyooka, Hyōgo|WD=Q696388|lt=Toyooka City}}, and {{ill|Kinosaki, Hyōgo|en|Kinosaki, Hyōgo|WD=Q6414198|lt=Kinosaki Town}}. Possessing a long history known since before the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian Period}}, it was called “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation” (海内第一泉) during the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo Period}}, a claim commemorated by an extant monument. Along with {{ill|Arima Onsen|en|Arima Onsen|WD=Q4790673|lt=Arima Onsen}} and {{ill|Yumura Onsen (Hyogo)|en|Yumura Onsen (Hyogo)|WD=Q8061163|lt=Yumura Onsen}}, it stands as one of Hyōgo Prefecture’s representative hot springs.
== Water Type == * {{ill|Brine spring|en|Brine spring|WD=Q11428612|lt=Salt Hot Spring}}: {{ill|Hot Spring Source|ja|源泉|1=Spring Mouth|1=Spring Mouth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Source|13=User:Immanuelle/Spring Mouth|qq=}} {{ill|Temperature|en|Temperature|WD=Q11466|lt=Temperature}} 37 – 83 {{ill|Celsius|en|Celsius|WD=Q25267|lt=Celsius}}. All the sources are collected in a centralized hot water distribution management facility built in 1972, where the average temperature is stabilized at 57°C, and then conveyed via a network of pipes to each {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|外湯|1=Sotoyu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Open-Air Bath|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotoyu|qq=}} and {{ill|Ryokan|en|Ryokan|WD=Q562930|lt=Ryokan}}.
== Onsen Town == [[File:161029 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan01s.jpg|left|thumb|Nighttime Onsen Town]]
Kinosaki Onsen is a hot spring town centered on a circuit of seven open-air baths. The foremost among these, {{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinoyu|1=Ichinoyu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17988814}}, was originally known in the Edo period as “Arayu” (新湯), but in mid-Edo, a practitioner of the {{ill|Kohō School|ja|古方派|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kohō School|1=Kohō school|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10913345}} of {{ill|Kampo Physician|ja|漢方医|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kampo Physician|1=Kampo physician|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11565521}} {{ill|Shūtoku Kagawa|ja|香川修徳|lt=Shūtoku Kagawa|lt_ja=香川修庵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shūtoku Kagawa|1=Kagawa Shūtoku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q6561882}} extolled its water quality and renamed it “Ichinoyu” to imply it was the best in the nation. Also, {{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satono-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540739}}—officially known as the Toyooka City Kinosaki Onsen Exchange Center—is managed under the designated administrator system, with its bathing and training facilities run as a public–private venture while other facilities remain municipal; its premises also house the Toyooka City Kinosaki General Branch Onsen Division. At the seven open-air baths established in the onsen town, a token called the “Ichiban-fuda” is distributed to the first bathers of the day.
An onsen town is formed along the banks of the {{ill|Daitanigawa|ja|大谿川|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daitanigawa|1=Ōtani River|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11439183}} (Ootani-gawa), which connects the seven open-air baths from right in front of {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|en|Kinosaki Onsen Station|WD=Q1055689|lt=Kinosaki Onsen Station}}, and along the riverbank, {{ill|Willow|ja|柳|lt=Willow|lt_ja=柳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Willow|1=柳|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15884500}} are planted. Lodging facilities also line the main stream of the {{ill|Maruyama River|en|Maruyama River|WD=Q11394765|lt=Maruyama River}} into which the Daitanigawa flows.<ref>[http://www.kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/shop/map.html 旅館・お店情報 » マップから探す] — Kinosaki Onsen Tourism Association (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> Moreover, the group of bridges spanning the Daitanigawa was designated as an {{ill|Important Structures for Landscape Formation|ja|景観形成重要建造物等 (兵庫県指定)|lt=Important Structures for Landscape Formation|lt_ja=景観形成重要建造物|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Important Structures for Landscape Formation|1=Important Structures for Landscape Formation|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514688}} by Hyōgo Prefecture in fiscal year Heisei 18 (2006). Located near the {{ill|Sea of Japan|en|Sea of Japan|WD=Q27092|lt=Sea of Japan}}, the hot spring is popular for {{ill|Sea bathing|en|Sea bathing|WD=Q1132965|lt=Sea Bathing}} in summer and for {{ill|Crab|en|Crab|WD=Q16033394|lt=Crab}} cuisine in winter. At Kinosaki Onsen Station, there is also Satono-yu (a hot spring facility within the station building) along with foot baths ({{ill|Ashiyu|en|Ashiyu|WD=Q725522|lt=Ashiyu}}) and hot spring drinking fountains ({{ill|Hot Spring Drinking Fountain|ja|飲泉|1=Hot Spring Drinking|de|Brunnenkur|lt=drinking hot spring|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Drinking Fountain|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Drinking|qq=}}), which are scattered throughout the town.
[[File:Kinosaki Onsen01s4592.jpg|thumb|Atago Bridge]]
At Kinosaki Onsen, wearing a {{ill|Yukata|en|Yukata|WD=Q849302|lt=Yukata}} with {{ill|Geta (footwear)|en|Geta (footwear)|WD=Q721941|lt=Geta}} is considered proper attire. As of 2007, most ryokan here provide a separate yukata for strolling the town—distinct from those used as nightwear ({{ill|Nightwear|ja|寝間着|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nightwear|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 寝巻|1=nightwear|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1187616}}) within the inn. Numerous shops in the town, identifiable by a signboard reading “Yukata Advisor,” (about 30 as of 2007) offer assistance when a guest’s yukata becomes disarranged, and some {{ill|Ashitaban|ja|下足番|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ashitaban|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 下駄箱|1=getabako|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2855743}} even lend their geta based on the design of the yukata.
A row of wooden, three‐story ryokan lines the street, and Toyooka City applies its {{ill|Landscape Ordinance|ja|景観条例|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Landscape Ordinance|1=Regulations of cityscape (in Japan)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514689}} to protect the area.<ref>[https://www.city.toyooka.lg.jp/shisei/keikaku/toshikeikaku/1003048/1003054.html 豊岡市城崎温泉地区における歴史的建築物の保存及び活用に関する条例] (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> In 2019, the commercial facility “{{ill|Nishimura Sanpō|ja|西村屋 (城崎温泉)|lt=Nishimura Sanpō|lt_ja=さんぽう西村屋本店|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nishimura Sanpō|1=Nishimuraya|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q105552895}},” established via a city-wide solicitation project, was designed with wooden exterior walls to harmonize with the townscape. As of 2019, there were 74 ryokan/hotels—most of which are small-scale, family-run establishments with fewer than 20 rooms—focusing on individual travelers. In 2018, approximately 630,000 tourists visited, including around 50,000 foreigners; the proportion of visitors from Europe, America, and Australia (predominantly individual travelers) was about 30%, higher than in other hot spring areas (approximately 10%). To increase the number of stays of two or more nights, comprehensive improvements to the onsen town—including its commercial facilities and the {{ill|Kinosaki International Art Center|ja|城崎国際アートセンター|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki International Art Center|1=Kinosaki International Arts Center|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q21652936}}—as well as cultural initiatives such as the “Books and Onsen” project (see below) have been implemented.
Additionally, a ropeway, {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Ropeway|1=Kinosaki Ropeway|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11426138}}, operates nearby, offering easy access to landmarks such as {{ill|Onsen Temple|ja|温泉寺 (豊岡市)|lt=Onsen Temple|lt_ja=温泉寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Temple|qq=}}, which is revered as the guardian temple of the Kinosaki Onsen area, and to the vicinity of the summit of Daishi Mountain where an observatory is located.
<gallery widths="160px" heights="110px"> Kinosaki onsen04 1920.jpg|Overview of the Onsen Town 一番札.jpg|Ichiban‑fuda 100722 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan03s3.jpg|Station Street Kinosaki onsen01 2816.jpg|Yunosato Street (the front right is “{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gyosho-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}”) </gallery>
== History == [[File:Kinosaki1noyu01 2816.jpg|thumb|The monument of Ichinoyu and “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation”]]
According to the {{ill|Hot Spring Founding Legend|ja|開湯伝説|1=Onsen Origin Myth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Founding Legend|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Origin Myth|qq=}}, in 629 during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|en|Emperor Jomei|WD=Q329761|lt=Emperor Shumei}}, the hot spring was discovered when a {{ill|Oriental stork|en|Oriental stork|WD=Q998495|lt=Stork}} was seen healing its wounds. In the early {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara Period}}, in 717 (the first year of the {{ill|Yōrō|en|Yōrō|WD=Q1373061|lt=Yōrō Era}}), the Buddhist monk {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōchi Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} chanted the Hachimandara Sutra for a thousand days to aid those suffering from incurable illnesses; as a result, in 720 (the fourth year of Yōrō) the sacred hot spring burst forth, marking the legendary beginning of Kinosaki Onsen. One of the seven open-air baths, {{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mandarayu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540745}}, was so named. Moreover, {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōchi Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} is also recognized as the founding priest ({{ill|Kaisan|en|Kaisan|WD=Q3191999|lt=Founding Priest}}) of Onsen Temple, which has since become a symbol of Kinosaki Onsen.
According to the Edo‑period {{ill|Onsen Ranking|ja|温泉番付|1=onsen banzuke|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Ranking|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Rankings|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11562960}}, Kinosaki Onsen was Ranked in the western division’s {{ill|Sekiwaki|ja|関脇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sekiwaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=sekiwake|WD=Q1937166}} (with the highest Rank being {{ill|Ozeki|ja|大関|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ozeki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=ōzeki|WD=Q2166602}}—the western Ozeki being {{ill|Arima Onsen|en|Arima Onsen|WD=Q4790673|lt=Arima Onsen}}). In that era, nine tubs served as the origin for the open‑air baths. {{ill|Kōgen Jōnin|ja|弘元上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōgen Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弘元|1=Kōgen Jōnin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q45830120}}, known as the “Kūkai of {{ill|Tajima Province|en|Tajima Province|WD=Q1053727|lt=Tajima Province}}” (referring to {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}}) and who served as the 50th and 52nd head of {{ill|Manpuku-ji|ja|満福寺 (養父市)|lt=Manpuku-ji|lt_ja=満福寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manpuku-ji|qq=}} in Tajima (and associated with {{ill|Mount Kōya|en|Mount Kōya|WD=Q535065|lt=Mount Kōya}}), was originally from the venerable ryokan {{ill|Yamamoto-ya|ja|山本屋|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamamoto-ya|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Kinosaki Onsen. During the {{ill|Bakumatsu|en|Bakumatsu|WD=Q804558|lt=Bakumatsu Period}}, {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|en|Kido Takayoshi|WD=Q696402|lt=Kido Takayoshi}} once fled to Kinosaki Onsen while pursued by the {{ill|Shinsengumi|en|Shinsengumi|WD=Q221031|lt=Shinsengumi}}. In the Edo period, Kinosaki Onsen featured not only entertainment venues but also numerous food establishments offering hot pot dishes, {{ill|Zenzai|ja|ぜんざい|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zenzai|1=zenzai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11270244}}, {{ill|Udon|en|Udon|WD=Q471861|lt=Udon}}, and {{ill|Soba|en|Soba|WD=Q753910|lt=Soba}}, while fruits, fish, and poultry were transported from afar, and even delicacies such as {{ill|Fugu|en|Fugu|WD=Q134385|lt=Pufferfish}}, {{ill|Octopus|en|Octopus|WD=Q40152|lt=Octopus}}, and {{ill|Duck|ja|鴨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Duck|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to カモ|1=duck|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3736439}} were available. Rental shops provided items including the {{ill|Shamisen|en|Shamisen|WD=Q241337|lt=Shamisen}}, {{ill|Sugoroku|en|Sugoroku|WD=Q1472906|lt=Sugoroku}}, {{ill|Go (board game)|ja|碁|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Go (board game)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 囲碁|1=go|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11413}}, {{ill|Biwa|ja|琵琶|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Biwa|1=pipa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q6685124}}, and {{ill|Koto|ja|琴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Koto|1=kin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11086494}}, as well as weapons like {{ill|Spear|en|Spear|WD=Q44475|lt=Spear}} and {{ill|Single-edged sword|en|Single-edged sword|WD=Q7523706|lt=Sword}}, delighting guests so thoroughly that they would forget to leave. Kinosaki Onsen was frequented by numerous feudal lords and retainers from neighboring domains, contributing to its lively atmosphere.
[[File:kinosaki_onsen.jpg|left|150px|thumb|Postcard from Meiji 43 (1910)]]
During the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|WD=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War}}, a convalescent home for wounded soldiers was established, which also ended the severe economic downturn that had persisted since the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|en|Meiji Restoration|WD=Q8707|lt=Meiji Restoration}}. In the ensuing Meiji era, many prominent literary figures—including {{ill|Naoya Shiga|en|Naoya Shiga|WD=Q957997|lt=Naoya Shiga}}, who wrote {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/In Kinosaki|1=At Kinosaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11425921}}, and {{ill|Takeo Arishima|en|Takeo Arishima|WD=Q577180|lt=Takeo Arishima}}—visited Kinosaki Onsen.
Around this time, the issue of private (inner) baths became prominent. In 1925 ({{ill|Taishō era|en|Taishō era|WD=Q329174|lt=Taisho Era}} 14), the town was completely destroyed in the {{ill|1925 North Tajima earthquake|en|1925 North Tajima earthquake|WD=Q11401118|lt=Northern Tajima Earthquake}}; of the approximately 1,200 bathers present, survivors fled along the tracks and were evacuated by rescue trains toward the Keihanshin region. By the following month, as many as 82 guests were already visiting Kinosaki, and as long as the hot spring flowed, the crowds never dwindled. Much of the current Japanese‑style wooden, three‑story townscape originates from the post‐earthquake reconstruction or from buildings of that era; until the earthquake, ryokan did not have private baths, and guests patronized the open‑air baths throughout the town. In 1927 ({{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Showa Era}} 2), when {{ill|Mikiya Ryokan|ja|三木屋|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikiya Ryokan|1=Mikiya|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q55533899}} (a lodging associated with {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/In Kinosaki|1=At Kinosaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11425921}}) utilized a newly discovered spring on its grounds to install the first private bath in a new building, legal disputes (the “Kinosaki Onsen Private Bath Lawsuit”) erupted over the perceived breach of local tradition, lasting more than 20 years. In 1950 (Showa 25), a settlement was reached allowing private baths with regulated size, while guests desiring larger communal baths continued to use the open‑air baths. Furthermore, all hot spring sources—including those on private property—were consolidated under the former Kinosaki Town “Yushima Zaisan‑ku,” and newly drilled sources began supplying private baths. In 1972, a centralized hot water distribution management facility—akin to a municipal water supply—was constructed to deliver water via pipes to each open‑air bath and ryokan.
[[File:Nishimuraya Hotel Shogetsutei Kinosaki Onsen Japan41s3.jpg|thumb|Private Bath (Reserved {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|露天風呂|1=Outdoor hot spring baths|1=Outdoor hot spring baths|ko|노천탕|1=Outdoor hot spring baths|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Open-Air Bath|13=User:Immanuelle/Outdoor hot spring baths|qq=}})]]
These reforms led to the widespread installation of private baths in ryokan; today, nearly all accommodations offer them, though even in large establishments their scale remains modest. Because guests are exempt from paying for open‑air baths, “open‑air bath tours” while clad in yukata have become a signature experience.
In 1963, the {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Ropeway|1=Kinosaki Ropeway|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11426138}} connecting the onsen town and the summit of Daishi Mountain was opened. In step with the period of high economic growth, a hot spring boom ensued, transforming Kinosaki Onsen into a major tourist destination. In July 2008, {{ill|Kiyamachi Lane|ja|木屋町小路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiyamachi Lane|1=Kiyamachi Kōji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11518305}} was opened on a passage linking Kiyamachi Street and {{ill|Shisho Shrine (Toyooka)|ja|四所神社 (豊岡市)|lt=Shisho Shrine|lt_ja=四所神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shisho Shrine (Toyooka City)|qq=}}. In January 2015, a fire broke out that resulted in two deaths and the complete loss of eight buildings ({{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Fire|ja|城崎温泉火災|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Onsen Fire|1=Kinosaki Onsen Fire|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24862932}}).
Toyooka DMO ({{ill|Destination marketing organization|en|Destination marketing organization|WD=Q3689421|lt=Tourism Regional Development Corporation}}), together with young ryokan managers and Toyooka City, established the Toyooka Tourism {{ill|Digital transformation|en|Digital transformation|WD=Q4252370|lt=Digital Transformation}} Promotion Council in 2021. This initiative shares non‑personal accommodation and reservation data to analyze where tourists originate and to forecast demand months in advance, thereby informing PR and pricing strategies.
== Management == Kinosaki Onsen is managed by the Yushima {{ill|Zaisan-ku|ja|財産区|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zaisan-ku|1=property ward|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q55521203}}, which not only owns four hot spring sources and six open‑air baths but also supplies hot spring water to 84 lodging facilities (for those outside the designated area, water is delivered by {{ill|Tank truck|en|Tank truck|WD=Q20465|lt=Tank Truck}}).<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXLASHD26H0U_W5A220C1AA1P00/ |title=外湯めぐりで共存共栄 歴史の遺物「財産区」(3) |publisher=日本経済新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref>
== Open‑Air Baths == === Seven Bath Circuit === The open‑air baths comprise the seven baths: '''{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinoyu|1=Ichinoyu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17988814}}''', '''{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gyosho-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540751}}''', '''{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mandarayu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540745}}''', '''{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satono-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540739}}''', '''{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yanagiyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540756}}''', '''{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jizoyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''', and '''{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Konoyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540761}}'''.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/about/spa/7onsen/ |title=城崎温泉 7つの外湯 |publisher=城崎温泉観光協会|accessdate=2022-05-21}}</ref>
<gallery> File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan03s3.jpg|{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinoyu|qq=}} – Renowned as “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation.” File:161030 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan04s3.jpg|{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gyosho-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – The bath of the elder sister of {{ill|Emperor Go-Horikawa|en|Emperor Go-Horikawa|WD=Q357221|lt=Emperor Gotohorikawa}}, known as {{ill|Princess Kuniko|en|Princess Kuniko|WD=Q6145785|lt=Yasuka Monin}}. File:Kinosaki mandarayu2816.jpg|{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mandarayu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – The bath associated with {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōchi Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, celebrated for a thousand days of sutra recitation. === Abolition of the Ichiban‑fuda === From 2002, the former Kinosaki Town Onsen Division and the Yushima Zaisan‑ku distributed an “Ichiban‑fuda” to the first man and woman to visit the open‑air baths each day.<ref name="kobe20210327">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/sougou/202103/0014188553.shtml |title=外湯巡りの「一番札」、人気で客が奪い合い 兵庫・城崎温泉やむなく廃止へ |publisher=神戸新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref> However, its overwhelming popularity led to disputes over order and even high‑priced listings on {{ill|Mercari|en|Mercari|WD=Q21019721|lt=Mercari}}, prompting the Yushima Zaisan‑ku to decide on its abolition at the end of March 2021.<ref name="kobe20210327"/>
Yushima Zaisan‑ku and others are now considering the planning and sale of commemorative items that can be purchased regardless of order.

== Books and Onsen == Among the noted literary figures, {{ill|Naoya Shiga|en|Naoya Shiga|WD=Q957997|lt=Naoya Shiga}} stayed for {{ill|Hot Spring Treatment|ja|湯治|1=thermal bath|2=ja|3=湯治|4=zh|5=湯治|6=ca|7=Termalisme|8=de|9=Thermalbad|10=es|11=Termalismo|13=Thermal bath|14=eo|15=Varmfonta banejo|16=fr|17=Thermalisme|18=la|19=Balneum thermale|20=lb|21=Thermalbad|22=hu|23=Termálfürdő|24=nl|25=Thermaalbad|26=pt|27=Turismo termal|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Treatment|13=User:Immanuelle/Thermal bath|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1004887}} due to an injury and wrote the {{ill|Short story|en|Short story|WD=Q49084|lt=Short Story}} {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/In Kinosaki|1=At Kinosaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11425921}}. In 2013, on the centennial of Shiga’s hot spring visit, the young proprietors of various ryokan at Kinosaki Onsen established a community‑rooted publishing label called “Books and Onsen”{{efn|August 20, 2013, certified as a {{ill|Specified Nonprofit Corporation|ja|特定非営利活動法人|lt=Specified Nonprofit Corporation|lt_ja=特定非営利活動法人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Specified Nonprofit Corporation|1=specified non-profit corporation|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11570934}} ({{Corporate Number|5140005021403}}).}}<ref>[http://books-onsen.com/ Books and Onsen] (accessed June 2018)</ref>. The first issue comprised two works by Shiga (“In Kinosaki” and its annotations); the second issue in 2014 was {{ill|Manjome Manabu|ja|万城目学|lt=Manjome Manabu|lt_ja=万城目学|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manjome Manabu|1=Manabu Makime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q9004033}}’s 『Kinosaki Trial』, and the third in 2016 was {{ill|Kanae Minato|en|Kanae Minato|WD=Q4390332|lt=Kanae Minato}}’s 『Returning to Kinosaki』. All new works, these have been released exclusively at the local ryokan. They are printed on highly water‑resistant stone paper—made not from wood {{ill|Pulp (paper)|en|Pulp (paper)|WD=Q672506|lt=Pulp}} or {{ill|Kenaf|en|Kenaf|WD=Q1137540|lt=Kenaf}}, but from an {{ill|Inorganic|ja|無機物|lt=Inorganic|lt_ja=無機物|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inorganic|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 無機化合物|1=inorganic compound|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q190065}} {{ill|Mineral|en|Mineral|WD=Q7946|lt=Mineral}} powder—with towels available as water‑repellent book covers. Additionally, the {{ill|Kinosaki Town Literary Museum|ja|城崎町文芸館|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Town Literary Museum|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 城崎文芸館|1=Kinosaki Bungeikan Heritage Museum|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11426143}}—opened in 1996—underwent a major renovation in 2016 for its 20th anniversary.

From Kōnotori Tajima Airport, it is a 40‑minute ride by airport bus to Kinosaki Onsen. ; Private Car * {{Ja Exp Route Sign|E27}}{{ill|Maizuru-Wakasa Expressway|en|Maizuru-Wakasa Expressway|WD=Q11613730|lt=Maizuru Wakasa Expressway}} at {{ill|Kasuga Interchange|ja|春日インターチェンジ|lt=Kasuga Interchange|lt_ja=春日インターチェンジ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Interchange|1=Kasuga interchange|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11088794}}, via the {{ill|Kitakinki-Toyooka Expressway|en|Kitakinki-Toyooka Expressway|WD=Q6157667|lt=Hokkin-Kinki Toyooka Expressway}}, {{ill|Japan National Route 312|en|Japan National Route 312|WD=Q6157205|lt=National Route 312}}, and {{ill|Hyōgo Prefectural Route 3 Toyooka Seto Line|ja|兵庫県道3号豊岡瀬戸線|lt=Hyōgo Prefectural Route 3 Toyooka Seto Line|lt_ja=兵庫県道3号豊岡瀬戸線|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hyōgo Prefectural Route 3 Toyooka Seto Line|1=Hyogo Prefectural Road Route 3|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11393412}}, etc.

{{Maplink2|zoom=13|frame=yes|frame-align=right|frame-width=300|coord={{coord|35|37|40|N|134|48|0|E}}|type=point}}
'''Kinosaki Onsen''' (城崎温泉) is a {{ill|Onsen|en|Onsen|WD=Q655311|lt=Onsen}} located in {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture}}, {{ill|Toyooka, Hyōgo|en|Toyooka, Hyōgo|WD=Q696388|lt=Toyooka City}}, and {{ill|Kinosaki, Hyōgo|en|Kinosaki, Hyōgo|WD=Q6414198|lt=Kinosaki Town}}. Possessing a long history known since before the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian Period}}, it was called “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation” (海内第一泉) during the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo Period}}, a claim commemorated by an extant monument. Along with {{ill|Arima Onsen|en|Arima Onsen|WD=Q4790673|lt=Arima Onsen}} and {{ill|Yumura Onsen (Hyogo)|en|Yumura Onsen (Hyogo)|WD=Q8061163|lt=Yumura Onsen}}, it stands as one of Hyōgo Prefecture’s representative hot springs.
== Water Type == * {{ill|Brine spring|en|Brine spring|WD=Q11428612|lt=Salt Hot Spring}}: {{ill|Hot Spring Source|ja|源泉|1=Spring Mouth|1=Spring Mouth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Source|13=User:Immanuelle/Spring Mouth|qq=}} {{ill|Temperature|en|Temperature|WD=Q11466|lt=Temperature}} 37 – 83 {{ill|Celsius|en|Celsius|WD=Q25267|lt=Celsius}}. All the sources are collected in a centralized hot water distribution management facility built in 1972, where the average temperature is stabilized at 57°C, and then conveyed via a network of pipes to each {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|外湯|1=Sotoyu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Open-Air Bath|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotoyu|qq=}} and {{ill|Ryokan|en|Ryokan|WD=Q562930|lt=Ryokan}}.
== Onsen Town == [[File:161029 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan01s.jpg|left|thumb|Nighttime Onsen Town]]
Kinosaki Onsen is a hot spring town centered on a circuit of seven open-air baths. The foremost among these, {{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinoyu|1=Ichinoyu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17988814}}, was originally known in the Edo period as “Arayu” (新湯), but in mid-Edo, a practitioner of the {{ill|Kohō School|ja|古方派|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kohō School|1=Kohō school|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10913345}} of {{ill|Kampo Physician|ja|漢方医|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kampo Physician|1=Kampo physician|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11565521}} {{ill|Shūtoku Kagawa|ja|香川修徳|lt=Shūtoku Kagawa|lt_ja=香川修庵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shūtoku Kagawa|1=Kagawa Shūtoku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q6561882}} extolled its water quality and renamed it “Ichinoyu” to imply it was the best in the nation. Also, {{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satono-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540739}}—officially known as the Toyooka City Kinosaki Onsen Exchange Center—is managed under the designated administrator system, with its bathing and training facilities run as a public–private venture while other facilities remain municipal; its premises also house the Toyooka City Kinosaki General Branch Onsen Division. At the seven open-air baths established in the onsen town, a token called the “Ichiban-fuda” is distributed to the first bathers of the day.
An onsen town is formed along the banks of the {{ill|Daitanigawa|ja|大谿川|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daitanigawa|1=Ōtani River|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11439183}} (Ootani-gawa), which connects the seven open-air baths from right in front of {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|en|Kinosaki Onsen Station|WD=Q1055689|lt=Kinosaki Onsen Station}}, and along the riverbank, {{ill|Willow|ja|柳|lt=Willow|lt_ja=柳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Willow|1=柳|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15884500}} are planted. Lodging facilities also line the main stream of the {{ill|Maruyama River|en|Maruyama River|WD=Q11394765|lt=Maruyama River}} into which the Daitanigawa flows.<ref>[http://www.kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/shop/map.html 旅館・お店情報 » マップから探す] — Kinosaki Onsen Tourism Association (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> Moreover, the group of bridges spanning the Daitanigawa was designated as an {{ill|Important Structures for Landscape Formation|ja|景観形成重要建造物等 (兵庫県指定)|lt=Important Structures for Landscape Formation|lt_ja=景観形成重要建造物|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Important Structures for Landscape Formation|1=Important Structures for Landscape Formation|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514688}} by Hyōgo Prefecture in fiscal year Heisei 18 (2006). Located near the {{ill|Sea of Japan|en|Sea of Japan|WD=Q27092|lt=Sea of Japan}}, the hot spring is popular for {{ill|Sea bathing|en|Sea bathing|WD=Q1132965|lt=Sea Bathing}} in summer and for {{ill|Crab|en|Crab|WD=Q16033394|lt=Crab}} cuisine in winter. At Kinosaki Onsen Station, there is also Satono-yu (a hot spring facility within the station building) along with foot baths ({{ill|Ashiyu|en|Ashiyu|WD=Q725522|lt=Ashiyu}}) and hot spring drinking fountains ({{ill|Hot Spring Drinking Fountain|ja|飲泉|1=Hot Spring Drinking|de|Brunnenkur|lt=drinking hot spring|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Drinking Fountain|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Drinking|qq=}}), which are scattered throughout the town.
[[File:Kinosaki Onsen01s4592.jpg|thumb|Atago Bridge]]
At Kinosaki Onsen, wearing a {{ill|Yukata|en|Yukata|WD=Q849302|lt=Yukata}} with {{ill|Geta (footwear)|en|Geta (footwear)|WD=Q721941|lt=Geta}} is considered proper attire. As of 2007, most ryokan here provide a separate yukata for strolling the town—distinct from those used as nightwear ({{ill|Nightwear|ja|寝間着|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nightwear|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 寝巻|1=nightwear|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1187616}}) within the inn. Numerous shops in the town, identifiable by a signboard reading “Yukata Advisor,” (about 30 as of 2007) offer assistance when a guest’s yukata becomes disarranged, and some {{ill|Ashitaban|ja|下足番|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ashitaban|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 下駄箱|1=getabako|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2855743}} even lend their geta based on the design of the yukata.
A row of wooden, three‐story ryokan lines the street, and Toyooka City applies its {{ill|Landscape Ordinance|ja|景観条例|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Landscape Ordinance|1=Regulations of cityscape (in Japan)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514689}} to protect the area.<ref>[https://www.city.toyooka.lg.jp/shisei/keikaku/toshikeikaku/1003048/1003054.html 豊岡市城崎温泉地区における歴史的建築物の保存及び活用に関する条例] (accessed 2019-09-29)</ref> In 2019, the commercial facility “{{ill|Nishimura Sanpō|ja|西村屋 (城崎温泉)|lt=Nishimura Sanpō|lt_ja=さんぽう西村屋本店|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nishimura Sanpō|1=Nishimuraya|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q105552895}},” established via a city-wide solicitation project, was designed with wooden exterior walls to harmonize with the townscape. As of 2019, there were 74 ryokan/hotels—most of which are small-scale, family-run establishments with fewer than 20 rooms—focusing on individual travelers. In 2018, approximately 630,000 tourists visited, including around 50,000 foreigners; the proportion of visitors from Europe, America, and Australia (predominantly individual travelers) was about 30%, higher than in other hot spring areas (approximately 10%). To increase the number of stays of two or more nights, comprehensive improvements to the onsen town—including its commercial facilities and the {{ill|Kinosaki International Art Center|ja|城崎国際アートセンター|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki International Art Center|1=Kinosaki International Arts Center|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q21652936}}—as well as cultural initiatives such as the “Books and Onsen” project (see below) have been implemented.
Additionally, a ropeway, {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Ropeway|1=Kinosaki Ropeway|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11426138}}, operates nearby, offering easy access to landmarks such as {{ill|Onsen Temple|ja|温泉寺 (豊岡市)|lt=Onsen Temple|lt_ja=温泉寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Temple|qq=}}, which is revered as the guardian temple of the Kinosaki Onsen area, and to the vicinity of the summit of Daishi Mountain where an observatory is located.
<gallery widths="160px" heights="110px"> Kinosaki onsen04 1920.jpg|Overview of the Onsen Town 一番札.jpg|Ichiban‑fuda 100722 Kinosaki Onsen Toyooka Hyōgo pref Japan03s3.jpg|Station Street Kinosaki onsen01 2816.jpg|Yunosato Street (the front right is “{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gyosho-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}”) </gallery>
== History == [[File:Kinosaki1noyu01 2816.jpg|thumb|The monument of Ichinoyu and “The Number One Hot Spring in the Nation”]]
According to the {{ill|Hot Spring Founding Legend|ja|開湯伝説|1=Onsen Origin Myth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Founding Legend|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Origin Myth|qq=}}, in 629 during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|en|Emperor Jomei|WD=Q329761|lt=Emperor Shumei}}, the hot spring was discovered when a {{ill|Oriental stork|en|Oriental stork|WD=Q998495|lt=Stork}} was seen healing its wounds. In the early {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara Period}}, in 717 (the first year of the {{ill|Yōrō|en|Yōrō|WD=Q1373061|lt=Yōrō Era}}), the Buddhist monk {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōchi Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} chanted the Hachimandara Sutra for a thousand days to aid those suffering from incurable illnesses; as a result, in 720 (the fourth year of Yōrō) the sacred hot spring burst forth, marking the legendary beginning of Kinosaki Onsen. One of the seven open-air baths, {{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mandarayu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540745}}, was so named. Moreover, {{ill|Dōchi Jōnin|ja|道智上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōchi Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} is also recognized as the founding priest ({{ill|Kaisan|en|Kaisan|WD=Q3191999|lt=Founding Priest}}) of Onsen Temple, which has since become a symbol of Kinosaki Onsen.
According to the Edo‑period {{ill|Onsen Ranking|ja|温泉番付|1=onsen banzuke|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Ranking|13=User:Immanuelle/Onsen Rankings|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11562960}}, Kinosaki Onsen was Ranked in the western division’s {{ill|Sekiwaki|ja|関脇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sekiwaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=sekiwake|WD=Q1937166}} (with the highest Rank being {{ill|Ozeki|ja|大関|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ozeki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=ōzeki|WD=Q2166602}}—the western Ozeki being {{ill|Arima Onsen|en|Arima Onsen|WD=Q4790673|lt=Arima Onsen}}). In that era, nine tubs served as the origin for the open‑air baths. {{ill|Kōgen Jōnin|ja|弘元上人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōgen Jōnin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弘元|1=Kōgen Jōnin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q45830120}}, known as the “Kūkai of {{ill|Tajima Province|en|Tajima Province|WD=Q1053727|lt=Tajima Province}}” (referring to {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}}) and who served as the 50th and 52nd head of {{ill|Manpuku-ji|ja|満福寺 (養父市)|lt=Manpuku-ji|lt_ja=満福寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manpuku-ji|qq=}} in Tajima (and associated with {{ill|Mount Kōya|en|Mount Kōya|WD=Q535065|lt=Mount Kōya}}), was originally from the venerable ryokan {{ill|Yamamoto-ya|ja|山本屋|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamamoto-ya|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} of Kinosaki Onsen. During the {{ill|Bakumatsu|en|Bakumatsu|WD=Q804558|lt=Bakumatsu Period}}, {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|en|Kido Takayoshi|WD=Q696402|lt=Kido Takayoshi}} once fled to Kinosaki Onsen while pursued by the {{ill|Shinsengumi|en|Shinsengumi|WD=Q221031|lt=Shinsengumi}}. In the Edo period, Kinosaki Onsen featured not only entertainment venues but also numerous food establishments offering hot pot dishes, {{ill|Zenzai|ja|ぜんざい|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zenzai|1=zenzai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11270244}}, {{ill|Udon|en|Udon|WD=Q471861|lt=Udon}}, and {{ill|Soba|en|Soba|WD=Q753910|lt=Soba}}, while fruits, fish, and poultry were transported from afar, and even delicacies such as {{ill|Fugu|en|Fugu|WD=Q134385|lt=Pufferfish}}, {{ill|Octopus|en|Octopus|WD=Q40152|lt=Octopus}}, and {{ill|Duck|ja|鴨|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Duck|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to カモ|1=duck|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3736439}} were available. Rental shops provided items including the {{ill|Shamisen|en|Shamisen|WD=Q241337|lt=Shamisen}}, {{ill|Sugoroku|en|Sugoroku|WD=Q1472906|lt=Sugoroku}}, {{ill|Go (board game)|ja|碁|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Go (board game)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 囲碁|1=go|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11413}}, {{ill|Biwa|ja|琵琶|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Biwa|1=pipa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q6685124}}, and {{ill|Koto|ja|琴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Koto|1=kin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11086494}}, as well as weapons like {{ill|Spear|en|Spear|WD=Q44475|lt=Spear}} and {{ill|Single-edged sword|en|Single-edged sword|WD=Q7523706|lt=Sword}}, delighting guests so thoroughly that they would forget to leave. Kinosaki Onsen was frequented by numerous feudal lords and retainers from neighboring domains, contributing to its lively atmosphere.
[[File:kinosaki_onsen.jpg|left|150px|thumb|Postcard from Meiji 43 (1910)]]
During the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|WD=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War}}, a convalescent home for wounded soldiers was established, which also ended the severe economic downturn that had persisted since the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|en|Meiji Restoration|WD=Q8707|lt=Meiji Restoration}}. In the ensuing Meiji era, many prominent literary figures—including {{ill|Naoya Shiga|en|Naoya Shiga|WD=Q957997|lt=Naoya Shiga}}, who wrote {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/In Kinosaki|1=At Kinosaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11425921}}, and {{ill|Takeo Arishima|en|Takeo Arishima|WD=Q577180|lt=Takeo Arishima}}—visited Kinosaki Onsen.
Around this time, the issue of private (inner) baths became prominent. In 1925 ({{ill|Taishō era|en|Taishō era|WD=Q329174|lt=Taisho Era}} 14), the town was completely destroyed in the {{ill|1925 North Tajima earthquake|en|1925 North Tajima earthquake|WD=Q11401118|lt=Northern Tajima Earthquake}}; of the approximately 1,200 bathers present, survivors fled along the tracks and were evacuated by rescue trains toward the Keihanshin region. By the following month, as many as 82 guests were already visiting Kinosaki, and as long as the hot spring flowed, the crowds never dwindled. Much of the current Japanese‑style wooden, three‑story townscape originates from the post‐earthquake reconstruction or from buildings of that era; until the earthquake, ryokan did not have private baths, and guests patronized the open‑air baths throughout the town. In 1927 ({{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Showa Era}} 2), when {{ill|Mikiya Ryokan|ja|三木屋|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikiya Ryokan|1=Mikiya|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q55533899}} (a lodging associated with {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/In Kinosaki|1=At Kinosaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11425921}}) utilized a newly discovered spring on its grounds to install the first private bath in a new building, legal disputes (the “Kinosaki Onsen Private Bath Lawsuit”) erupted over the perceived breach of local tradition, lasting more than 20 years. In 1950 (Showa 25), a settlement was reached allowing private baths with regulated size, while guests desiring larger communal baths continued to use the open‑air baths. Furthermore, all hot spring sources—including those on private property—were consolidated under the former Kinosaki Town “Yushima Zaisan‑ku,” and newly drilled sources began supplying private baths. In 1972, a centralized hot water distribution management facility—akin to a municipal water supply—was constructed to deliver water via pipes to each open‑air bath and ryokan.
[[File:Nishimuraya Hotel Shogetsutei Kinosaki Onsen Japan41s3.jpg|thumb|Private Bath (Reserved {{ill|Open-Air Bath|ja|露天風呂|1=Outdoor hot spring baths|1=Outdoor hot spring baths|ko|노천탕|1=Outdoor hot spring baths|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Open-Air Bath|13=User:Immanuelle/Outdoor hot spring baths|qq=}})]]
These reforms led to the widespread installation of private baths in ryokan; today, nearly all accommodations offer them, though even in large establishments their scale remains modest. Because guests are exempt from paying for open‑air baths, “open‑air bath tours” while clad in yukata have become a signature experience.
In 1963, the {{ill|Kinosaki Ropeway|ja|城崎ロープウェイ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Ropeway|1=Kinosaki Ropeway|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11426138}} connecting the onsen town and the summit of Daishi Mountain was opened. In step with the period of high economic growth, a hot spring boom ensued, transforming Kinosaki Onsen into a major tourist destination. In July 2008, {{ill|Kiyamachi Lane|ja|木屋町小路|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kiyamachi Lane|1=Kiyamachi Kōji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11518305}} was opened on a passage linking Kiyamachi Street and {{ill|Shisho Shrine (Toyooka)|ja|四所神社 (豊岡市)|lt=Shisho Shrine|lt_ja=四所神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shisho Shrine (Toyooka City)|qq=}}. In January 2015, a fire broke out that resulted in two deaths and the complete loss of eight buildings ({{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Fire|ja|城崎温泉火災|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Onsen Fire|1=Kinosaki Onsen Fire|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24862932}}).
Toyooka DMO ({{ill|Destination marketing organization|en|Destination marketing organization|WD=Q3689421|lt=Tourism Regional Development Corporation}}), together with young ryokan managers and Toyooka City, established the Toyooka Tourism {{ill|Digital transformation|en|Digital transformation|WD=Q4252370|lt=Digital Transformation}} Promotion Council in 2021. This initiative shares non‑personal accommodation and reservation data to analyze where tourists originate and to forecast demand months in advance, thereby informing PR and pricing strategies.
== Management == Kinosaki Onsen is managed by the Yushima {{ill|Zaisan-ku|ja|財産区|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zaisan-ku|1=property ward|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q55521203}}, which not only owns four hot spring sources and six open‑air baths but also supplies hot spring water to 84 lodging facilities (for those outside the designated area, water is delivered by {{ill|Tank truck|en|Tank truck|WD=Q20465|lt=Tank Truck}}).<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXLASHD26H0U_W5A220C1AA1P00/ |title=外湯めぐりで共存共栄 歴史の遺物「財産区」(3) |publisher=日本経済新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref>
== Open‑Air Baths == === Seven Bath Circuit === The open‑air baths comprise the seven baths: '''{{ill|Ichinoyu|ja|一の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichinoyu|1=Ichinoyu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17988814}}''', '''{{ill|Gyosho-yu|ja|御所の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gyosho-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540751}}''', '''{{ill|Mandarayu|ja|まんだら湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mandarayu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540745}}''', '''{{ill|Satono-yu|ja|さとの湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satono-yu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540739}}''', '''{{ill|Yanagiyu|ja|柳湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yanagiyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540756}}''', '''{{ill|Jizoyu|ja|地蔵湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jizoyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}''', and '''{{ill|Konoyu|ja|鴻の湯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Konoyu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135540761}}'''.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://kinosaki-spa.gr.jp/about/spa/7onsen/ |title=城崎温泉 7つの外湯 |publisher=城崎温泉観光協会|accessdate=2022-05-21}}</ref>

=== Abolition of the Ichiban‑fuda === From 2002, the former Kinosaki Town Onsen Division and the Yushima Zaisan‑ku distributed an “Ichiban‑fuda” to the first man and woman to visit the open‑air baths each day.<ref name="kobe20210327">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/sougou/202103/0014188553.shtml |title=外湯巡りの「一番札」、人気で客が奪い合い 兵庫・城崎温泉やむなく廃止へ |publisher=神戸新聞|accessdate=2021-03-27}}</ref> However, its overwhelming popularity led to disputes over order and even high‑priced listings on {{ill|Mercari|en|Mercari|WD=Q21019721|lt=Mercari}}, prompting the Yushima Zaisan‑ku to decide on its abolition at the end of March 2021.<ref name="kobe20210327"/>
Yushima Zaisan‑ku and others are now considering the planning and sale of commemorative items that can be purchased regardless of order.

based on wikidata|WD=Q1883600}}, {{ill|Mukai Kyorai|en|Mukai Kyorai|WD=Q541000|lt=Kurai Mukai}}, {{ill|Kunio Yanagita|en|Kunio Yanagita|WD=Q971687|lt=Kunio Yanagida}}, {{ill|Yosano Akiko|en|Yosano Akiko|WD=Q464104|lt=Akiko Yosano}}, and {{ill|Tekkan Yosano|en|Tekkan Yosano|WD=Q1206405|lt=Tekkkan Yosano}}.
== Local Characters == * {{ill|Matsuba Crab|ja|松葉カニ|lt=Matsuba Crab|lt_ja=松葉カニ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuba Crab|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}: Joe (younger brother) and Saki (older sister) * {{ill|Oriental stork|en|Oriental stork|WD=Q998495|lt=Stork}}: Shō-kun and Mai-chan (a couple) * {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Senchitai Onsenja|ja|城崎泉隊オンセンジャー|lt=Kinosaki Onsen Senchitai Onsenja|lt_ja=城崎泉隊オンセンジャー|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Onsen Senchitai Onsenja|1=Kinosaki Sentai Onsenger|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11426139}} (Sotoy Red, Yukata Blue, Mugi Wry Yellow) * The evil organization Hedarark (General Kigawaru, the Bath Tub Monster Skahn, the PRankster Koujagero, Chokkai)
== Books and Onsen == Among the noted literary figures, {{ill|Naoya Shiga|en|Naoya Shiga|WD=Q957997|lt=Naoya Shiga}} stayed for {{ill|Hot Spring Treatment|ja|湯治|1=thermal bath|2=ja|3=湯治|4=zh|5=湯治|6=ca|7=Termalisme|8=de|9=Thermalbad|10=es|11=Termalismo|13=Thermal bath|14=eo|15=Varmfonta banejo|16=fr|17=Thermalisme|18=la|19=Balneum thermale|20=lb|21=Thermalbad|22=hu|23=Termálfürdő|24=nl|25=Thermaalbad|26=pt|27=Turismo termal|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hot Spring Treatment|13=User:Immanuelle/Thermal bath|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1004887}} due to an injury and wrote the {{ill|Short story|en|Short story|WD=Q49084|lt=Short Story}} {{ill|In Kinosaki|ja|城の崎にて|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/In Kinosaki|1=At Kinosaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11425921}}. In 2013, on the centennial of Shiga’s hot spring visit, the young proprietors of various ryokan at Kinosaki Onsen established a community‑rooted publishing label called “Books and Onsen”{{efn|August 20, 2013, certified as a {{ill|Specified Nonprofit Corporation|ja|特定非営利活動法人|lt=Specified Nonprofit Corporation|lt_ja=特定非営利活動法人|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Specified Nonprofit Corporation|1=specified non-profit corporation|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11570934}} ({{Corporate Number|5140005021403}}).}}<ref>[http://books-onsen.com/ Books and Onsen] (accessed June 2018)</ref>. The first issue comprised two works by Shiga (“In Kinosaki” and its annotations); the second issue in 2014 was {{ill|Manjome Manabu|ja|万城目学|lt=Manjome Manabu|lt_ja=万城目学|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manjome Manabu|1=Manabu Makime|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q9004033}}’s 『Kinosaki Trial』, and the third in 2016 was {{ill|Kanae Minato|en|Kanae Minato|WD=Q4390332|lt=Kanae Minato}}’s 『Returning to Kinosaki』. All new works, these have been released exclusively at the local ryokan. They are printed on highly water‑resistant stone paper—made not from wood {{ill|Pulp (paper)|en|Pulp (paper)|WD=Q672506|lt=Pulp}} or {{ill|Kenaf|en|Kenaf|WD=Q1137540|lt=Kenaf}}, but from an {{ill|Inorganic|ja|無機物|lt=Inorganic|lt_ja=無機物|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inorganic|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 無機化合物|1=inorganic compound|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q190065}} {{ill|Mineral|en|Mineral|WD=Q7946|lt=Mineral}} powder—with towels available as water‑repellent book covers. Additionally, the {{ill|Kinosaki Town Literary Museum|ja|城崎町文芸館|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinosaki Town Literary Museum|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 城崎文芸館|1=Kinosaki Bungeikan Heritage Museum|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11426143}}—opened in 1996—underwent a major renovation in 2016 for its 20th anniversary.

Bus * From {{ill|Kyōto Station|en|Kyōto Station|WD=Q801046|lt=Kyoto Station}}, {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|WD=Q35765|lt=Osaka City}} (via {{ill|Hankyu Sanbancho Express Bus Terminal|ja|阪急三番街高速バスターミナル|lt=Hankyu Sanbancho Express Bus Terminal|lt_ja=阪急三番街高速バスターミナル|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hankyu Sanbancho Express Bus Terminal|1=Hankyu Highway Bus Osaka-Umeda Terminal|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11656774}}), and {{ill|Kobe|en|Kobe|WD=Q48320|lt=Kobe City}} (via {{ill|Sannomiya Station Bus Stop|ja|三宮駅バスのりば#神姫バス神戸三宮バスターミナル|lt=Sannomiya Station Bus Stop|lt_ja=三宮駅バスのりば|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sannomiya Station Bus Stop|1=Sannomiya Station Bus Stop|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11355154}}), take the {{ill|Zentan Express Bus|ja|全但特急バス|lt=Zentan Express Bus|lt_ja=全但特急バス|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zentan Express Bus|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} to get off at either {{ill|Kinosaki Onsen Station|en|Kinosaki Onsen Station|WD=Q1055689|lt=Kinosaki Onsen Station}} or “Kinosaki Onsen”. ; From Kōnotori Tajima Airport, it is a 40‑minute ride by airport bus to Kinosaki Onsen. ; Private Car * {{Ja Exp Route Sign|E27}}{{ill|Maizuru-Wakasa Expressway|en|Maizuru-Wakasa Expressway|WD=Q11613730|lt=Maizuru Wakasa Expressway}} at {{ill|Kasuga Interchange|ja|春日インターチェンジ|lt=Kasuga Interchange|lt_ja=春日インターチェンジ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Interchange|1=Kasuga interchange|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11088794}}, via the {{ill|Kitakinki-Toyooka Expressway|en|Kitakinki-Toyooka Expressway|WD=Q6157667|lt=Hokkin-Kinki Toyooka Expressway}}, {{ill|Japan National Route 312|en|Japan National Route 312|WD=Q6157205|lt=National Route 312}}, and {{ill|Hyōgo Prefectural Route 3 Toyooka Seto Line|ja|兵庫県道3号豊岡瀬戸線|lt=Hyōgo Prefectural Route 3 Toyooka Seto Line|lt_ja=兵庫県道3号豊岡瀬戸線|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hyōgo Prefectural Route 3 Toyooka Seto Line|1=Hyogo Prefectural Road Route 3|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11393412}}, etc.
